articles.title: Node.js Isn't Single-Threaded. How libuv and the OS Kernel Actually Run Your Code.
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute architectural deep dive into Node.js runtime internals. Learn how V8, the libuv threadpool, OS kernel event demultiplexers (epoll/kqueue/IOCP), the 6-phase event loop, and Worker Threads execute JavaScript under the hood.
articles.body_html:
Ask almost any software engineer how Node.js works, and you will hear the exact same sentence repeated like a universal law of physics:

"Node.js is single-threaded."

It is written in conference slides, repeated in job interviews, and taught in beginner bootcamps across the globe.

Yet if you start a basic Node.js HTTP server on a Linux machine and inspect the process with ps -eLf or htop, you will see something that immediately shatters that mental model:

Your single Node.js process is running eight or more native operating system threads simultaneously.

If Node.js were truly single-threaded:

  • Encrypting passwords with crypto.pbkdf2 would freeze your entire backend until the hash finished computing.
  • Reading a 4-gigabyte file from disk with fs.readFile would block every incoming HTTP request on your server.
  • Compressing response payloads with zlib would cause global latency spikes for all concurrent users.

None of those operations freeze your server.

The truth is that Node.js has never been a simple single-threaded program.

Node.js is a multi-threaded C and C++ runtime engine that presents a single-threaded JavaScript execution interface to developer code.

Underneath your JavaScript functions sits an intricate coordination machine powered by Google's V8 engine, the libuv cross-platform abstraction library, and operating system kernel primitives that have evolved over three decades.

To build fast, resilient, and non-blocking production backends, you have to look past the "single-threaded" slogan and understand how Node.js actually runs your code.

Here is what is really happening beneath your call stack.

The Three Tiers of Node.js: V8, libuv, and the Kernel

To see where the threads actually live, we need to decompose a Node.js process into its three distinct architectural layers.

[ Your JavaScript Code ]
          │
          ▼
[ Tier 1: Google V8 Engine ] ── Single-Threaded Call Stack & Heap
          │
          ▼
[ Tier 2: libuv Runtime ]   ── Event Loop + 4x Worker Threadpool
          │
          ▼
[ Tier 3: OS Kernel ]       ── Non-Blocking Sockets (epoll / kqueue / IOCP)

Tier 1: The JavaScript Execution Context (V8 Engine)

This is the only part of Node.js that is truly single-threaded.

Google's V8 engine executes your application code, user-defined functions, object allocations, and variable assignments within a single execution thread called the Main Thread.

Because the main thread executes one stack frame at a time, synchronous JavaScript loops (while (true) {}) or expensive recursive calculations will monopolize the CPU and starve the rest of your application.

Tier 2: The libuv Asynchronous Engine

When your JavaScript code calls an asynchronous Node.js API (such as reading a file, computing a hash, or resolving a domain name), V8 does not execute the underlying operating system call.

Instead, V8 passes the request across internal C++ bindings into libuv.

libuv is a high-performance C library originally built specifically for Node.js (and now also used by Julia and other languages).

libuv maintains two primary tools:

  1. The Event Loop: A single-threaded state machine that orchestrates callbacks and timers.
  2. The Worker Threadpool: A pool of pre-spawned background OS threads (defaulting to 4 threads) used to run blocking operations completely off the main thread.

Tier 3: The Operating System Kernel Subsystem

Here lies the biggest revelation in Node.js systems architecture:

Network I/O does not use the libuv worker threadpool at all.

When you create an HTTP server, connect to a PostgreSQL database, or open a WebSocket, your operating system kernel handles the network sockets through native event demultiplexers:

  • Linux: epoll
  • macOS and BSD: kqueue
  • Windows: IOCP (I/O Completion Ports)

These kernel subsystems monitor tens of thousands of network sockets concurrently without allocating a single OS thread.

File System I/O vs Network I/O: The Architectural Split

One of the most persistent misconceptions is that all asynchronous Node.js operations work the same way under the hood.

In reality, Node.js handles file system operations and network sockets through completely separate execution pipelines.

Why File I/O Requires Background Threads

Consider this common code:

import fs from 'node:fs';

fs.readFile('/var/log/app.log', (err, data) => {
  console.log('File read complete:', data.length);
});

Why does this asynchronous call require background threads?

Because across most operating systems (particularly Linux), there is no truly non-blocking API for regular disk file operations.

While network sockets can easily report whether incoming data is ready to be read, standard file systems on physical disk drives do not provide a universal, non-blocking asynchronous event interface.

If Node.js called read() on a disk file from the main V8 thread, and the hard drive heads had to seek across physical disk platters or wait for a network-mounted volume (NFS/EFS), the main thread would freeze for milliseconds. No HTTP requests could be handled during that pause.

To prevent this freeze:

  1. fs.readFile() packages the file descriptor and buffer into a work request (uv_work_t).
  2. libuv places the request into an internal task queue.
  3. An idle worker thread from the libuv threadpool picks up the request.
  4. The worker thread calls the blocking C system call read() entirely in the background.
  5. Once the bytes are read into memory, the worker thread posts a completion event back to the event loop.
  6. The main thread picks up the completion event during the Poll phase and invokes your JavaScript callback.

Why Network I/O Never Touches the Threadpool

Now look at an incoming HTTP request or an outgoing API fetch:

import http from 'node:http';

http.get('http://api.example.com/users', (res) => {
  res.on('data', (chunk) => {
    console.log('Received packet chunk');
  });
});

Does this operation take a thread from the libuv worker threadpool?

No. It consumes zero worker threads.

Network sockets are represented by file descriptors that support non-blocking mode. When Node.js creates a socket, it flags the socket as non-blocking:

// libuv sets O_NONBLOCK on socket file descriptors
fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, O_NONBLOCK);

Then, libuv registers the socket descriptor with the OS kernel's event demultiplexer (epoll_ctl on Linux).

The kernel's network stack monitors the physical Network Interface Card (NIC). When packets arrive over the wire, the hardware fires an interrupt, the kernel fills an internal buffer, and epoll marks the socket descriptor as readable.

libuv simply asks the kernel: "Which of our 20,000 registered sockets have data ready right now?"

The kernel returns the ready list instantly. Node.js reads the bytes and executes your callback, all without burning background worker threads.

This fundamental distinction explains why a single Node.js instance can easily hold 50,000 idle WebSocket connections open, yet simultaneously struggle if 10 threads attempt heavy cryptographic hashing at the same time.

The 6 Discrete Phases of the libuv Event Loop

Many developers picture the event loop as a basic JavaScript array of functions:

// The false mental model
while (queue.length > 0) {
  const callback = queue.shift();
  callback();
}

In the actual C implementation of libuv (src/unix/core.c), the event loop is a structured, six-phase state machine. Each phase maintains its own queue of pointers to C callbacks and operates on strict rules.

Here is what happens during each tick of the loop:

1. Timers Phase

The loop begins by checking for expired timers scheduled via setTimeout() and setInterval().

libuv stores active timers in a binary min-heap sorted by expiration timestamp. During this phase, libuv compares the current system clock with the root of the heap. It loops through all timers whose target time has arrived, executing their associated JavaScript callbacks in order.

2. Pending Callbacks (I/O Callbacks Phase)

This phase executes deferred system callbacks that were postponed from the previous loop iteration.

For instance, if a TCP socket connection attempt fails with an operating system error like ECONNREFUSED, some UNIX platforms report the error asynchronously. libuv defers reporting the error until this phase to give the system time to stabilize.

3. Idle / Prepare Phase

These two phases are used internally by libuv for housekeeping and synchronization before polling. Developer code cannot schedule callbacks directly into these queues.

4. Poll Phase: The Heart of Node.js

The Poll phase is where Node.js spends the vast majority of its operational life.

The Poll phase performs two critical responsibilities:

  1. It calculates how long it should block and wait for new I/O events.
  2. It processes ready events from the kernel demultiplexer (epoll_wait).

If the poll queue contains events (such as incoming network packets or completed file read operations from the threadpool), libuv iterates through them and executes their JavaScript callbacks synchronously.

What happens if the poll queue is empty?

  • If callbacks are scheduled in the setImmediate() queue (the Check phase), Node.js does not wait. It ends the Poll phase immediately and proceeds to Check.
  • If timers are pending in the Timers phase, libuv blocks only for the exact amount of time remaining until the earliest timer expires.
  • If no timers and no setImmediate calls are pending, libuv blocks indefinitely until the OS kernel signals that a network packet has arrived!

5. Check Phase (setImmediate)

The Check phase exists exclusively to execute callbacks registered via setImmediate().

Because the Check phase runs immediately after the Poll phase, setImmediate() callbacks are guaranteed to run right after incoming I/O events are processed, before the loop cycles back to check timers again.

6. Close Callbacks Phase

If a socket or stream is abruptly destroyed (such as socket.destroy() or socket.on('close')), its cleanup handler executes during this final phase, freeing allocated C structures before the next tick begins.

The Microtask Interceptors: process.nextTick vs Promises

Notice that neither process.nextTick() nor Promise.then() appeared in the six libuv phases above.

Why?

Because Microtasks are not part of the libuv event loop at all. They belong to the V8 engine layer.

Microtasks do not wait for the event loop to advance to a specific phase. Instead, they act as high-priority interceptors that run immediately after the current operation finishes, between every single callback, and at every phase boundary.

The Two Microtask Queues

Node.js manages two distinct microtask queues in memory:

  1. The process.nextTick Queue: Maintained internally by Node.js. It holds callbacks scheduled via process.nextTick().
  2. The Promise Microtask Queue: Maintained by the V8 engine. It holds resolved Promise callbacks (.then(), .catch(), await continuations, and queueMicrotask()).

The Strict Priority Ladder

Whenever the V8 JavaScript call stack empties:

  1. Node.js processes the nextTick queue until it is completely drained.
  2. Node.js processes the Promise microtask queue until it is completely drained.
  3. Only after both queues are empty does libuv resume executing the active phase of the event loop.

Consider this classic interview puzzle:

console.log("1: Synchronous");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("2: setTimeout");
}, 0);

setImmediate(() => {
  console.log("3: setImmediate");
});

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log("4: Promise Microtask");
});

process.nextTick(() => {
  console.log("5: process.nextTick");
});

console.log("6: Synchronous End");

Here is the exact execution trace:

  1. console.log("1: Synchronous") executes on the call stack.
  2. setTimeout(..., 0) registers a timer in libuv's min-heap.
  3. setImmediate(...) queues a callback in libuv's Check phase queue.
  4. Promise.resolve().then(...) queues a callback in the V8 Promise microtask queue.
  5. process.nextTick(...) queues a callback in the nextTick queue.
  6. console.log("6: Synchronous End") executes on the call stack.
  7. The call stack is now empty. Before the event loop can proceed, the microtask interceptor runs:
    • It checks the nextTick queue: prints "5: process.nextTick".
    • It checks the Promise queue: prints "4: Promise Microtask".
  8. The event loop now begins. Depending on machine speed and process startup latency, the Timers phase or Check phase executes next, printing either 2 or 3.

The Starvation Hazard

Because process.nextTick drains completely before any event loop phase can continue, recursive nextTick calls will completely freeze your server:

function starveLoop() {
  process.nextTick(starveLoop); // Danger: Infinite recursion in microtask queue
}
starveLoop();

In this scenario, the Poll phase is never reached. Incoming HTTP requests, database responses, and file read operations are starved indefinitely. The server is completely paralyzed without throwing an error.

Threadpool Starvation: The Silent Performance Killer

Now let us examine what happens when developers run CPU-intensive tasks on Node.js without realizing they are sharing a tiny worker pool.

By default, the libuv threadpool size is set to 4 threads:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE = 4

These 4 threads are shared across:

  • All fs file system calls (fs.readFile, fs.writeFile, fs.stat)
  • Asynchronous cryptography (crypto.pbkdf2, crypto.scrypt, crypto.randomBytes)
  • Compression routines (zlib.gzip, zlib.brotliCompress)
  • DNS resolution via dns.lookup (which uses the blocking POSIX getaddrinfo() C library)

The Latency Spike Experiment

Imagine a Node.js authentication service that hashes passwords using crypto.pbkdf2:

import crypto from 'node:crypto';

function hashPassword(password) {
  const start = Date.now();
  crypto.pbkdf2(password, 'salt', 100_000, 64, 'sha512', () => {
    console.log(`Hash finished in ${Date.now() - start}ms`);
  });
}

// Five users attempt to log in at the exact same millisecond:
hashPassword('pass1');
hashPassword('pass2');
hashPassword('pass3');
hashPassword('pass4');
hashPassword('pass5');

If you run this code, you will observe an alarming result:

Hash finished in 82ms   // Request 1 (Thread 1)
Hash finished in 84ms   // Request 2 (Thread 2)
Hash finished in 85ms   // Request 3 (Thread 3)
Hash finished in 86ms   // Request 4 (Thread 4)
Hash finished in 168ms  // Request 5 (Queued!)

Requests 1 through 4 finish in roughly 84 milliseconds.

Request 5 takes twice as long (168 ms), even though all five requests do the exact same amount of work!

Why?

Because the threadpool only has 4 threads. Requests 1 through 4 monopolized every worker thread simultaneously. Request 5 sat completely frozen in the libuv task queue, waiting for one of the first four threads to finish before it could even begin computing.

Worse, while those 4 threads were computing hashes:

  • Any concurrent fs.readFile() on your server had to wait in the queue.
  • Any dns.lookup() domain resolution had to wait in the queue.
  • Your entire backend experienced sudden, mysterious latency spikes.

The Production Fix

You can increase the size of the worker threadpool up to 128 threads by setting the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable:

UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=16 node server.js

Crucial Caveat: You must set this environment variable before the Node.js process starts. Setting process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE = 16 inside your JavaScript code will not work, because libuv initializes its threadpool during C startup before your script runs!

Modern Concurrency: Worker Threads & SharedArrayBuffer

Increasing UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE helps with I/O and native cryptography, but what if you need to run heavy JavaScript calculations (like parsing large JSON dumps, generating PDF reports, or running machine learning algorithms)?

JavaScript still executes on the single main V8 thread. Increasing the libuv threadpool will not help.

This is why Node.js introduced the worker_threads module.

Worker threads provide true CPU multi-threading inside Node.js by spinning up separate V8 instances on independent operating system threads.

Method 1: MessagePort & Structured Cloning

The standard way to communicate between worker threads is via parentPort.postMessage():

// main.js
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';

const worker = new Worker('./heavy-task.js', {
  workerData: { items: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] }
});

worker.on('message', (result) => {
  console.log('Calculation complete:', result);
});

Under the hood, postMessage uses the HTML Structured Clone Algorithm.

It serializes the JavaScript object, copies the data across the thread boundary, and deserializes a fresh copy inside the worker thread's private memory heap.

This approach provides total memory isolation and zero risk of race conditions. However, if you pass a 500-megabyte dataset between threads, the serialization and copying overhead will consume substantial CPU time and memory.

Method 2: Zero-Copy Concurrency with SharedArrayBuffer & Atomics

For maximum performance, modern Node.js allows multiple worker threads to point directly to the exact same physical memory address using SharedArrayBuffer:

// main.js
import { Worker } from 'node:worker_threads';

// Allocate 1 kilobyte of shared physical RAM
const sharedBuffer = new SharedArrayBuffer(1024);
const sharedInts = new Int32Array(sharedBuffer);

const worker = new Worker('./worker.js', {
  workerData: { sharedBuffer }
});

// Wait for worker to signal update
Atomics.wait(sharedInts, 0, 0);
console.log('Worker updated index 0 to:', sharedInts[0]);

In the worker thread:

// worker.js
import { workerData } from 'node:worker_threads';

const sharedInts = new Int32Array(workerData.sharedBuffer);

// Mutate memory directly with atomic safety
Atomics.store(sharedInts, 0, 42);
Atomics.notify(sharedInts, 0, 1); // Wake up waiting main thread

With SharedArrayBuffer:

  • Zero data is copied or serialized.
  • Both the main thread and the worker thread read and write to the exact same RAM bytes.
  • The Atomics object provides thread-safe operations (load, store, add, wait, notify), preventing data races and corrupted memory states.

This transforms Node.js from a simple event-driven script runner into a high-concurrency systems platform capable of high-throughput numerical processing.

Architectural Takeaways for Production Backends

When you step back and look at the entire machine, the true architecture of Node.js becomes clear:

  1. JavaScript is single-threaded; Node.js is not. The V8 engine executes user code on a single thread, while libuv and the OS kernel handle concurrency with multiple native background threads.
  2. Network I/O is non-blocking at the kernel level. Sockets rely on epoll, kqueue, and IOCP, consuming zero worker threads and enabling immense network concurrency.
  3. File I/O and crypto rely on the libuv threadpool. A default pool of 4 threads means concurrent file reads or hashing operations can easily cause silent queuing bottlenecks.
  4. Microtasks take absolute priority. process.nextTick() and Promise callbacks run between every phase boundary. Recursive nextTicks will starve the event loop completely.
  5. Worker Threads unlock true CPU parallelism. For heavy CPU workloads, offload calculations to dedicated worker_threads using structured messaging or lock-free SharedArrayBuffer memory.

Node.js achieved its dominance not because single-threaded execution is inherently superior, but because its creators built a brilliant bridge between an intuitive, single-threaded developer model and the multi-threaded, asynchronous power of modern operating systems.

When you architect your next Node.js microservice or debug a mysterious production latency spike, which layer of the runtime usually causes the most surprises in your codebase? And how do you balance worker thread pools against external worker queues like Redis or BullMQ in your infrastructure?

References & Technical Standards:

  • libuv Official Architecture & Design Guide
  • Node.js Official Documentation: The Event Loop, Timers, and process.nextTick()
  • Node.js Core Repository: C++ libuv Integration & fs Implementation
  • Google V8 Engine Documentation: Memory Heap & Concurrency
  • POSIX Standards: Non-blocking I/O and epoll(7) Linux Programmer's Manual

articles.title: 🏢 Ever Fluorescent: Project Plan and Debrief
articles.description: This is going to cover a lot, and I will do my best to keep it brief. Thank you for following the...
articles.body_html:
This is going to cover a lot, and I will do my best to keep it brief. Thank you for following the journey of an independent artist powering through the web. Small, but mighty. ⚡

Last night I had one of those nights where my brain just refused to shut off, despite being tired. This is pretty rare for me, I like the peace that comes with sleeping, and the bed can be a very strong magnet.

Before I fell asleep, I decided I was a project manager, and that my entire strategy needed a facelift.

As solo developer, I leaned into claude to sort out my 9,000 thoughts.

🏹 Strengths: Creativity, drive, ideas, writing, communication, time management, learning, technical skills, inspiring others, general management, and life administration.

⬇️ Weaknesses: Deviating from plans, emotions, self doubt, and other anxieties

👾 Claudinarian

Something clicked in my brain last night. I thought to myself: “This project is so vast that I need A project manager and another developer so that I can run things.” 🤣I sat with that idea for a bit, feeling overwhelmed. I gave some thought to what my real issues were on a very deep and personal level. I reflected on my own existence.

I decided to organize my thoughts with Claude, as is my go-to. I have become quite the claudinarian. Having messed with the “Projects” feature of claude before, the multi-agent bot with an orchestrator at the top, I knew the most appropriate manner to share my thoughts. I had previously gotten lost with this feature in the sub-bots and frequently lost my place and it was very confusing. Having that experience I knew I had to approach claude with targeted, specific and detailed requests. This way, claude would send a minion to do the bidding. Once that started, I could return to claude boss to place a new request. I think I’ve got it figured out now, I won't navigate to a minion and try to complete a project from a sub-agent (Guilty!)

As each task completed, I had Claude build me and artifact for that area of focus. I was creating and collecting organized documentation for myself so I could build a legitimate project plan with enough work to keep me busy for literally weeks.

How it started

The original plan was to optimize SEO, after having been absolutely devastated by my website performance (yes, I felt like a failure for a second “wow, how do I suck that bad? I try so hard!”) 😂

In my previous post, I shared a redirect disaster created from years of doing things on the web for my business as a non-developer. I had made a giant mess for myself. I’m sure if I went to a 'professional' they would have said something like “Here is the rebranding plan for your new business…” not wanting to deal with my disaster. Good thing I started learning web development a few years ago! I have gained so many skills that will be useful for running my small business. Monumentally powerful and not something that too many CEOs can say they can do themselves. Maniacal Laughter

Side tangent again. 😂 pivot Too many redirects in my brain.

First Task

SO, I have boss claude and the minion claudettes doing some legwork. This is my team for the night. Before I created the first task, I did some personal research. After fixing the redirect problem, I investigated my accessibility features to keep it clean. (I had recently completed a formal webdev class and the accessibility stuff was fresh in my head). everfluorescent.com came out mostly good, but I created a To-Do list and added that to it. No big deal, I can handle that.

With redirects created properly, canonical set as it should be and a decent user-friendliness score, I proceeded to run everfluorescent.com through multiple SEO checkers. They returned mixed results as expected. Here is some free ones I used that you may find useful:

  • SEOptimizer (Full audit)
  • Open Graph Preview Tool (Found no share image)
  • SEObility.net (Came back with on-page score of 87%)
  • SavageAudit (85/100 overall - details locked)

Savage Audit is awesome even on the free tier. Look what it said 🤣

I fed claude the data from all 4 sources, I told it to use it as a reference to build my plan.

This morning, I still had a bajillion tabs open and I noticed something. Before implementing the next wave of SEO optimization (not the first time I’m doing this), my average rank in searches was at position 5.3. 5.3!!!! That’s the first page of a Google Search! Boss.

My indexing is currently being fixed as well. As you can see from the chart below, the trends are now moving in the right direction. Redirects improving, proper canonical tag, and 404s have trended downward as well. This is excellent news.

Second Task

Diving into the problem of reach is next. This is something that I am not surprised about. Due to personal reasons, I had basically ghosted all of my social medias for the last few years. This is a significant area of pain for my brand and shop. (This was one of those situations where personal life disintegrated work life, I would always get compliments at live events, and it was very difficult to stop doing it.) I came up with a plan to create 365 days of unique content. Posting will be set to semi automatic. This will undoubtedly be a tremendous amount of work, but luckily I am mostly ready to take on the challenge.

Before I do that I will collect all of my information from wherever it lives, and I will have lots of stories to tell and share with the world about my brand, experiences, and travels. I'm not sure what provoked me at midnight last night. Perhaps a small inner voice silently screaming: "Move woman! You can cover a lot of ground quickly now!"

Third Task

Rebranding and breathing life back into a business is no easy task, that is what the importance of the regular scheduled content creation is. The plan is to cleanup security and management features on all social medias (I did this a while back, but it's going to get rechecked and updated with a tedious checklist!) I will use an external free tool for scheduled content posting. (Metricool fits the bill at the moment) This way, I can rest assured that my brand and content is being shared without needing to take so much time out everyday for posting and managing social media.

24 hours of evidence!

With some of the most severe issues addressed, It appears that I am already heading in the right direction! The chart does not lie.

I just checked my Google analytics and here is the story:

Things are looking up, and we are getting back on the right track. I've still got a monumental amount of work to do, but one thing at a time. I don't want to get excited over some 'blip anomaly' and I'm going to watch it like an obsessed hawk for a while.

Man, I'm so pleased to see that line finally peeled itself off the floor in google analytics!

Thank you for sharing my excitement and reading my post! <3

articles.title: The Most Embarrassing Private Key in Web PKI History
articles.description: The strange thing about this incident is that the certificates looked normal.  They had familiar CA...
articles.body_html:
The strange thing about this incident is that the certificates looked normal.

They had familiar CA names. They chained to trusted roots. Browsers could validate them. Audit cycles came and went.

But eight eMudhra intermediate certificates had a private key problem so severe that it did not need a supercomputer, a quantum breakthrough, or a clever cryptographic attack.

The private key could be recovered by counting.

That is the story behind the eMudhra CA incident. It is a cryptography failure, but it is also an operational failure, a review failure, and an incident-handling failure.

The public picture is still incomplete. eMudhra has said its final root-cause analysis is still in progress, so this article separates confirmed facts from the likely failure chain described in public reporting.

The short version

On April 30, 2025, a key-generation ceremony produced weak private keys for eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra.

The affected certificates used elliptic-curve cryptography. A secure P-384 private key should be a huge random number. The affected values were reportedly below 256. One widely discussed example was a key with the value 4.

That is not “a little weak.” It is equivalent to leaving a four-digit-looking combination lock on a vault that was supposed to have hundreds of digits of randomness.

The public certificates contained the matching public keys. Anyone could take the public key, try the small possible private values, and recover the private key in under a second.

The weak intermediates were publicly trusted for about 18 months. A researcher reported the issue to the Chrome Root Program on October 17, 2026. Chrome and Firefox blocked the affected certificates quickly. eMudhra revoked the intermediates and later announced customer migration support.

No public evidence currently shows that the weak keys were exploited before disclosure. That is good news. It does not make the incident small.

First, what does an intermediate CA actually do?

Most people meet certificate authorities only when a browser shows a padlock. Behind that padlock is a chain of trust.

Trusted root CA
      ↓ signs
Intermediate CA
      ↓ signs
Website or code-signing certificate
      ↓
Browser, device, or application accepts the certificate

The root CA is the high-value trust anchor. Browsers and operating systems keep it in a root store. The root normally stays protected and signs intermediate CAs instead of signing every website certificate itself.

The intermediate CA is the day-to-day issuer. It can sign certificates for websites, software publishers, and other use cases allowed by its constraints.

That is why an intermediate private key matters so much. If an attacker has it, they may be able to create certificates that look legitimate to software that trusts the chain.

This is not about compromising one website. It is about compromising a machine that can make many websites or signed programs look trustworthy.

Why the key being “4” changes everything

For an elliptic-curve key, the public key is calculated from the private key using this relationship:

Q = d × G

Where:

  • d is the private key
  • G is a public, fixed base point for the curve
  • Q is the public key placed in the certificate

With a normal P-384 key, d should be a random value with roughly 384 bits of entropy. The point of elliptic-curve cryptography is that, given a normal public key Q, working backward to find d is infeasible.

But that promise has a condition: the private key has to be random and huge.

If d is less than 256, an attacker does not need to solve a hard math problem. They can calculate:

1 × G
2 × G
3 × G
4 × G
...
255 × G

Then they compare each result to the public key in the certificate. The match reveals the private key.

This is why the failure is so startling. The cryptographic algorithm did not suddenly become weak. The key generation process supplied it with a private value so small that the algorithm never had a chance to provide security.

What public reporting says went wrong

The public account points to a stacked failure, not a single accidental click.

According to eMudhra’s statements and public incident discussions:

  1. The ceremony was intended to generate proper RSA-4096 and P-384 key pairs for a set of intermediates.
  2. A ceremony deviation introduced a wrap-and-unwrap test for HSM key handling.
  3. A flaw in the ceremony script produced a second set of weak EC keys alongside the expected keys.
  4. The weak and strong key sets were labelled similarly.
  5. The wrong key objects were selected when certificate-signing requests were created.
  6. The resulting weak public keys were signed into intermediate CA certificates and cross-signed for compatibility.
  7. The strong keys remained on the HSM but were not the keys represented by the published certificates.

The exact root cause is still not final. That matters. It would be wrong to pretend that a public timeline tells us every detail of an internal ceremony, every review, or every decision.

But the important shape is already visible:

a generation defect created bad keys, then a selection and verification failure published them.

Either failure by itself could have been caught. Together, they became a browser-trust incident.

The warning that should have stopped everything

The most uncomfortable part of the public account is not the original scripting mistake. It is what reportedly happened a few weeks later.

Around May 2025, certificate revocation list signatures began failing verification.

A CRL is a signed list of certificates that should no longer be trusted. For the signature to validate, the private key used to sign the CRL must match the public key in the issuing CA certificate.

If that check fails, the system is telling you something specific:

The private key signing this CRL does not match
the public key advertised in this CA certificate.

For a CA, that should be an incident. Not a ticket to close after a configuration tweak.

Public reporting says the CRL signer was reconfigured to use the weak key set, which made the signatures verify. That removed the immediate symptom. It did not answer why two different key sets existed or why the published certificate did not match the expected HSM signing key.

This is the difference between making an alarm stop and finding out why it rang.

The missed RCA, step by step

An RCA is not a paragraph that says “wrong key was configured.” A useful RCA keeps asking until it reaches a broken control, not just the person or configuration nearest the failure.

Here is what a shallow analysis might look like:

Stage Shallow answer
Symptom CRL signatures do not verify
Immediate cause The signer is using the wrong key
Fix Point the signer at the other key
Status Closed

That is not enough, because it accepts the existence of the extra key as normal.

Here is the harder, more useful line of questioning:

Question What the investigation should establish
Why did the CRL signature fail? The signer private key did not match the public key in the intermediate certificate.
Why did they not match? The certificate request used a different key pair than the intended HSM signing key.
Why were there two key pairs? The ceremony produced extra key material during the wrap-and-unwrap test.
Why did the wrong one get selected? Labels and selection controls did not make the intended key unambiguous.
Why did nobody catch the mismatch before issuance? There was no independent post-ceremony reconciliation proving that each certificate request matched the intended HSM key.

At the second question, the incident was already discoverable.

Someone could have compared the public-key fingerprint in the certificate request with the public-key fingerprint of the HSM object. They could have inspected the key properties. They could have run a basic sanity test against the EC public point.

Any of those checks could have converted a future ecosystem-wide incident into a re-ceremony while the keys were still internal.

Why two audits did not catch it

It is tempting to hear “two audit cycles” and conclude that audits are useless. That is not the lesson.

Audits are usually designed to verify that documented controls exist and are being followed. They may witness a ceremony, sample records, review approvals, and inspect procedures. They do not necessarily recompute the security properties of every generated cryptographic key.

That gap matters here.

A ceremony can have the right people in the room, the right forms, the right HSM, and the right signatures on a checklist while still publishing a catastrophically weak key. Process evidence is not the same as cryptographic validation.

For a CA, the validation needs to include the key material itself:

  • Does the certificate request public key match the intended HSM key by fingerprint?
  • Is there exactly one approved key pair per intended intermediate?
  • Does the EC public key pass a small-scalar sanity check?
  • Do all generated key objects reconcile to the ceremony plan?
  • Has an independent tool verified the output rather than the ceremony script verifying its own work?

These are inexpensive checks compared with the cost of removing a root from browser stores.

Why revocation was not enough

eMudhra revoked the affected intermediates. That was necessary. It was not sufficient.

Revocation works only when clients fetch revocation information and decide to enforce it. Some clients do this consistently. Some soft-fail during network errors. Some do not check at all.

Browsers have additional mechanisms. Chrome and Firefox can push emergency distrust information much faster than waiting for every client to download and honour a CRL. That explains how the affected intermediates were blocked quickly after the report.

But a CA key that was publicly trusted through multiple paths needs a response that reaches more than browsers.

The affected intermediates also had cross-signed copies under Sectigo’s AAA Certificate Services. Cross-signing exists for a reasonable compatibility goal: older devices may trust the cross-signing root even when they do not have a newer eMudhra root.

In this case, compatibility became a risk multiplier.

Same weak intermediate key
        ↙                    ↘
eMudhra trust path      Sectigo cross-signed path

Blocking only the eMudhra path would not necessarily stop a client from accepting a chain through the other path. That is why browsers also had to address the cross-signed route.

Browsers were not the only thing to think about

Browser blocks are visible and fast. Backend clients are quieter.

Command-line tools, internal services, custom mobile applications, embedded devices, Java runtimes, private trust stores, and applications with pinned or stale CA bundles may not receive the same emergency protection on the same timeline.

They can also behave differently around Certificate Transparency and revocation checks.

The practical lesson for engineering teams is simple:

Do not disable certificate validation because a trust-chain migration caused a connection failure.

That turns a compatibility problem into a security bypass.

If a service breaks because a CA chain is no longer trusted, update the service’s certificates, trust store, client library, or configuration correctly. A temporary “verify false” setting is the kind of workaround that creates the next incident.

What a CA should change after this

The interesting controls here are not exotic.

1. Reconcile the ceremony output

After any key ceremony, list every HSM key object and compare it to the approved plan. There should be exactly one expected key pair per CA identity. Extra or unexpected key objects should stop the process.

2. Select keys by fingerprint, not a friendly label

Names can be similar. Operators can misread them. A SHA-256 fingerprint tied to the ceremony record is much harder to confuse.

3. Verify public keys independently

Use a separate tool and a separate reviewer to confirm that the certificate request’s public key matches the approved HSM object. The same ceremony script should not be the only thing vouching for its own result.

4. Test key quality before signing

For EC keys, check for obvious small-scalar values. For RSA keys, perform the appropriate checks for weak or shared factors. The CA should test its own signing keys at least as carefully as it tests customer certificate requests.

5. Treat unexplained crypto failures as incidents

A signature verification failure involving a CA key needs documented root cause, preserved evidence, and independent review before closure. “It works after we changed the key” is the start of an investigation, not the end.

6. Review ceremony deviations as security changes

A wrap-and-unwrap test sounds narrow. It touches secret-key handling, which makes it a security-critical change. It should have separate review, a dry run on a non-production HSM, and an output check that is independent of the changed script.

7. Re-check cross-signed intermediates

Cross-signing changes who can trust a key. Every new trust path should trigger the same key-quality verification and an explicit answer to the question: “How do we block this key everywhere if something goes wrong?”

What this means for everyone else

Most teams are not CA operators. The useful lessons still transfer.

Security checks are signals, not annoyances

If an integrity check fails, do not make it pass by changing the validation path until you understand the mismatch. The most expensive incidents often start as a warning that somebody classified as annoying.

Your automation needs an independent check

Automation is good at repeating a bad decision very quickly. When it creates credentials, certificates, signing keys, backups, or access controls, validate the output with a separate tool or control plane.

Know your trust dependencies

Every outbound HTTPS client depends on certificate validation. Inventory which applications use custom trust stores, pinned certificates, old Java bundles, embedded firmware, or unusual proxy settings before an emergency forces the question.

Rotation speed is a security control

Fast key and certificate rotation is not just convenient. It determines whether a trust incident lasts hours, days, or months.

What is still unknown

There are important open questions, and it is worth keeping them open until primary evidence answers them:

  • eMudhra’s final root-cause analysis and independent expert review
  • the exact ceremony-code defect and the controls that allowed it through
  • the complete internal handling of the May 2025 CRL signature failures
  • whether any client populations outside browser protections accepted chains from the affected keys
  • the final scope of browser and operating-system trust-store actions

Public reporting currently says there is no known exploitation before disclosure, and Chrome reported no logged TLS certificates from the six affected TLS intermediates before its block. Those facts reduce the known impact. They do not reduce the urgency of learning from the control failure.

The real headline

The headline is not that elliptic-curve cryptography failed.

It is that a security system relied on several layers of trust, yet none of those layers asked the simplest possible question soon enough:

“Does the public key we published actually belong to the secure private key we meant to use?”

For a CA, that question should be impossible to skip.

For everyone else, this is a reminder that strong cryptography only starts with the algorithm. It survives or fails based on generation, labelling, verification, review, monitoring, and how seriously teams take the first warning.

Sources

  • eMudhra certificate security incident statement
  • Cisco Talos: Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates
  • Encryption Consulting: When the CA Key Was 4
  • Mozilla Bugzilla incident 2083449

articles.title: I deleted the mail server from my VPS and got 1.2 GB of RAM back
articles.description: So I run ExtraTime, it's a football trivia site with daily puzzles, the Grid game, multiplayer rooms...
articles.body_html:
So I run ExtraTime, it's a football trivia site with daily puzzles, the Grid game, multiplayer rooms and leaderboards and so on. Backend is Django on one VPS with 8 GB RAM, frontend is Next.js on Vercel. Pretty normal side project setup that kind of grew bigger than I planned.

Until this October the same VPS was also running my own mail server, and I want to write down how I moved off it to smtpfa.st, because honestly it went way better than I expected, and the part where stuff broke was actually the best part (I'll explain).

Nobody asked me to write this post. I'm writing it because I think how it went is worth sharing with other people who self-host their mail without really needing to.

How it was before

When I started I thought email is something I should just own myself, how hard can it be? So I put docker-mailserver in a container next to the app, then a SnappyMail container on top so I can read admin@ from the browser, and then a whole separate git repo only for the mail config. Django sent through it on port 587.

It worked, mostly. But when I actually looked inside the container this October it was running Postfix, Dovecot, rspamd for spam, ClamAV for viruses (just the signature database was 309 MB on disk), and fail2ban because ports 25, 587 and 993 were open to the internet and the bots found them quickly. All of this so my site can send password reset emails and verification links to people, which is the most basic thing an app does.

docker stats showed the mailserver using 1.14 GiB. The same box runs Postgres, Redis, gunicorn, daphne for the websockets, Prometheus and some exporters, so 1.14 GiB for a thing that does nothing most of the day felt wasteful. Early October I was looking where to free some memory and the first idea was to turn ClamAV off, and then I thought, if I'm touching the mail server anyway why not just remove the whole thing and use a proper service.

The RAM was honestly not even the main problem for me. The main problem was I had zero visibility, if a reset email didn't arrive I had no idea if it went to spam or bounced or the address was fake or what. There was no dashboard, no events, nothing I could connect Django to. DMARC was on p=none and the reports were going to a mailbox that I almost never opened.

Plus I wanted to start a newsletter, and sending a newsletter from your own Postfix on a VPS IP address is a pretty good way to get that IP on a blocklist.

Account emails first

This part was boring, in a good way.

smtpfa.st has an SMTP relay so for Django it's only settings, and the password is an API key that can only send:

EMAIL_HOST = "smtp.smtpfa.st"
EMAIL_PORT = 587
EMAIL_USE_TLS = True
EMAIL_HOST_USER = "smtpfast"
EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD = env("EMAIL_HOST_PASSWORD")  # send-only key

I added their DNS records in Cloudflare, the dashboard showed everything verified, I sent a password reset to myself and it was there in Gmail and in the smtpfa.st logs. That was it.

One thing I didn't know: smtpfa.st treats mail that comes over SMTP as marketing by default, unless you say it isn't. Makes sense because they add the unsubscribe headers and respect opt-outs, but a password reset obviously has to arrive even if the person unsubscribed from the newsletter. There is a header for this, so I made a small email backend that puts it on every email Django sends:

from django.core.mail.backends.smtp import EmailBackend

CATEGORY_HEADER = "X-SMTPfast-Category"
UNTRACKED_HEADERS = {
    "X-SMTPfast-Track-Clicks": "false",
    "X-SMTPfast-Track-Opens": "false",
}


class TransactionalEmailBackend(EmailBackend):
    def send_messages(self, email_messages):
        for message in email_messages or ():
            message.extra_headers.setdefault(CATEGORY_HEADER, "transactional")
            for header, value in UNTRACKED_HEADERS.items():
                message.extra_headers.setdefault(header, value)
        return super().send_messages(email_messages)

They read the headers and remove them before sending. The two tracking headers I added a few days later, there's a story behind those further down.

The newsletter

This is really why I did the whole thing. ExtraTime has around 2,200 registered players from the last few years and I had literally no way to tell them when we add something new, except a banner on the site that only people already on the site will see.

What I ended up with: Django is the source of truth for consent. You turn product emails on or off in your profile and a nightly job syncs that to the contacts in smtpfa.st, and if they ever disagree Django wins. The email templates are React Email in the frontend repo with the same Tailwind colours as the site, a build step turns them to HTML and uploads them as hosted templates, so the emails actually look like ExtraTime and not like some generic template.

Broadcasts I create with the REST API. When we launched country variations for the Grid I didn't want people in Brazil getting the email at 4 in the morning, so the audience got split by country and time zone, which ended up being 18 scheduled broadcasts for one campaign (a bit much, in hindsight). Now I do one batch per day at 10:00 Sofia time and it's much simpler.

Unsubscribes, spam complaints and bounces come back to Django as webhooks, signed with HMAC-SHA256, so verifying is short:

def signature_is_valid(body, header):
    secret = settings.SMTPFAST_WEBHOOK_SECRET
    if not secret or not header:
        return False
    expected = hmac.new(secret.encode(), body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    received = header.strip().removeprefix("sha256=")
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected.encode(), received.encode("utf-8", "replace"))

Every event is saved by its id first so if they retry it nothing happens twice. And for people without an account there's a hosted sign-up form with double opt-in, the /newsletter page on our site posts straight to it and smtpfa.st sends the confirmation mail.

I built most of this with Claude Code, and smtpfa.st has an MCP server and a skill file for agents, which helped more than I thought it would, because the agent was reading the real API response shapes and not guessing them.

Bounces (my fault, not theirs)

First campaign I sent to everyone who was opted in, and a lot of them had not logged in for years. The bounce rate went to 3.9%, and sending gets paused at 5%, and soft bounces count too, not only hard ones. Not a fun number to watch climb.

But this was entirely on me. smtpfa.st showed exactly which addresses bounced and the reason, mostly typos and dead domains from old signups. After that I made a rule that any address that bounces even once never gets mailed again, and we check the MX records too so dead domains get removed before the first send. If you are about to email an old user list for the first time, clean it first.

When stuff broke

This is the part that made me want to write all this.

On October 10, the first day, I hit a bunch of small problems while building everything above, so I wrote them all down and sent them to smtpfa.st support. The same evening I got a reply that started with "Everything you reported is fixed and live now" and a list. Marketing and transactional mail got split, so an unsubscribe doesn't block password resets anymore (that's where the header above comes from). Suppressions now show the reason why an address is blocked. There was a paging bug where contacts in a segment could repeat or disappear because the sort had no tiebreaker, fixed. Tags started coming back on GET /v1/emails/:id, and the docs got the real webhook payloads and bounce types.

Next morning two more things were live, send_over_minutes for spreading a broadcast over a few hours, and custom link domains so the tracking and unsubscribe links use your own hostname. I added one CNAME for a subdomain of extratime.world and the certificate just appeared on its own.

On the 12th I noticed the links inside password reset emails were going through the click tracker. Those links have single-use tokens in them and I really didn't like that they pass through a redirect, so I asked if I can turn tracking off for single emails. First answer was that none of the options exist yet but they will add them. Second answer came the same afternoon and all four were live: SMTP headers, API fields, an account switch for transactional mail, and an attribute for single links. That's the X-SMTPfast-Track-* thing in my backend.

After that I started reporting things as GitHub issues, and the timestamps tell the story better than I can:

Issue Opened Fix PR Closed
#841 Contacts stat boxes weren't clickable filters Oct 14, 07:56 UTC 23 min later ~3 h
#842 No way to archive sent broadcasts Oct 14, 07:59 UTC ~1.5 h later ~3 h
#853 MCP OAuth rejected Claude Code's localhost callback Oct 16, 08:50 UTC 10 min later 20 min

853 is my favourite. Claude Code uses a random localhost port for the OAuth callback and their server only accepted the exact redirect that was registered, so connecting failed. I opened the issue and it was fixed 20 minutes later.

I've worked with the big email providers before and you know how that goes, ticket, auto-reply, and after a week someone says it's on the roadmap. This was nothing like that.

Removing the old server

When everything was going through smtpfa.st, removing the old mail server was quick. I backed up the two mailboxes (less than 200 KB each, which tells you how much I actually used them), stopped and deleted the mailserver and SnappyMail containers, closed 25, 587 and 993 in the firewall, removed the VPS IP from the SPF record, and pointed MX to Cloudflare Email Routing which forwards everything to my Gmail.

Used RAM went from 5,537 MB to 4,322 MB. And it's one repo less, three ports less, and no more ClamAV updating its signatures in the middle of the night for an inbox nobody reads.

So would I recommend it

Yes. It's a young service and in the first weeks you could tell: when I started only the CLI was public, and the dashboard had some rough spots, two of which are in the table above. That moved fast too. There are now official SDKs for Node, Python, Go and PHP, plus a Laravel package and a Terraform provider. But the sending, the webhooks and the docs have been solid for me, and I have never had a provider fix things this fast.

If you are still running Postfix next to your app only for password resets, you probably don't need to.

And if you like football come play the daily Grid on ExtraTime. The newsletter will tell you when there's something new, and this time I can actually see if it arrived.

articles.title: Shipping Flutter Web to Firebase When Your GitHub Actions Budget Hits Zero
articles.description: On October 18, right in the middle of shipping a multi-feature audit and a supplement tracker...
articles.body_html:
On October 18, right in the middle of shipping a multi-feature audit and a supplement tracker redesign on my personal life_os_app (my daily Flutter Web + Cloud Firestore operating board), GitHub Actions stopped scheduling jobs. The billing meter for my personal account's hosted runner minutes had hit 100%.

Look at what my .github/workflows/ci.yml and deploy-live.yml were doing on every push and pull request:

  1. Spinning up an ubuntu-latest VM.
  2. Pulling the Flutter SDK and warming the Pub cache (~90s).
  3. Installing Python 3 and running 68 CLI sync unit tests (~15s).
  4. Running flutter analyze and 466 widget and accessibility tests (~110s).
  5. Compiling flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn (~140s).
  6. Authenticating via Workload Identity Federation (google-github-actions/auth@v2) and deploying to Firebase Hosting target board (~35s).

That is 6.5 minutes per PR push and another 4 minutes on merge to main. Across 70+ PRs in October, a single-developer personal project burned through thousands of CI minutes doing work my local Apple Silicon MacBook finishes in under 35 seconds.

When your CI budget hits zero on a personal repo, you have two choices: pay for extra runner minutes to compile code your laptop already compiled, or build a deterministic local verification and deployment pipeline that is faster and safer than the YAML workflow it replaces.

Here is the exact architecture I use to keep life_os_app shipping to Firebase Hosting and Cloud Firestore with zero GitHub Actions spend.

Architecture: The Three-Layer Local Verification Gate

Moving deploys to your local machine only works if you never deploy unverified state. In life_os_app, the application state is split across two runtimes:

  • Python 3.14 CLI Sync Tools (tool/board_*.py): Morning and evening scripts that pull from Apple Reminders, Google Calendar, Harvest, Notion, and GCP Billing, then write structured JSON documents into Cloud Firestore over REST.
  • Flutter Web Client (lib/): A Riverpod 3 + Material 3 multi-skin web app served from Firebase Hosting with a custom offline Service Worker (web/offline-sw.js).

Layer 1: Firestore Schema Validation Before Every REST Write

One of the biggest risks of running CLI sync tools outside a container is accidentally clobbering fields that the Flutter Web client writes directly from the browser. For example, on the Events and Admin tabs, I tick tasks directly in the UI (config/events.taskTicks and config/admin.done), while tool/board_events.py and tool/board_admin.py sync metadata from Notion and GCP Billing.

To prevent a CLI run from wiping browser taps, tool/board_firestore.py enforces two rules before any HTTP PATCH leaves the machine:

  1. Explicit schema validation on every collection (dayPlans, stats, config, finance, plan).
  2. Field-level update masks (?updateMask.fieldPaths=...) plus hard blocks against overwriting client-owned map keys: 
# tool/board_firestore.py
if path == "config/events" and "taskTicks" in data and not fields:
    raise SystemExit(
        "refusing to overwrite config/events.taskTicks without --fields; "
        "pass --fields updated,source,events"
    )
if path == "config/admin" and "done" in data and not fields:
    raise SystemExit(
        "refusing to overwrite config/admin.done without --fields"
    )

In addition, caching the gcloud auth print-access-token call with @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1) and enforcing a 15-second socket timeout cut multi-document Firestore sync latency by 80% and eliminated hanging background processes when switching Wi-Fi networks.

Layer 2: Per-Document Decode Isolation in Flutter Streams

In Cloud Firestore, a single malformed field inside one historical document in a collection query (collection('dayPlans').snapshots()) will normally throw a FormatException or TypeError inside .map(), killing the entire StreamProvider and replacing your UI with an error state.

During my audit pass, I hardened every repository to isolate decoding per document:

// lib/features/day_board/data/board_repository.dart
List<T> _decodeEach<T>(
  QuerySnapshot<JsonMap> query,
  T Function(JsonMap data, String id) decode,
) {
  final results = <T>[];
  for (final doc in query.docs) {
    try {
      results.add(decode(doc.data(), doc.id));
    } on Object catch (error, stackTrace) {
      developer.log(
        'Skipping malformed document ${doc.reference.path}',
        name: 'day_board.repository',
        error: error,
        stackTrace: stackTrace,
      );
    }
  }
  return results;
}

When saving multi-day edits (such as editing 7 days of focus blocks and habit notes in the This Week sheet), replacing 14 sequential await set() calls with a single atomic WriteBatch (saveWeekEditsBatch) eliminated partial-save race conditions on flaky mobile connections.

Layer 3: Self-Contained Web Bundles (--no-web-resources-cdn) & Service Worker Cleanup

When deploying Flutter Web to Firebase Hosting for daily use on iPhone, iPad, and desktop, CDN font/CanvasKit fetches can stall on airplane or train Wi-Fi. Building with --no-web-resources-cdn bundles CanvasKit and font assets directly into build/web/, paired with a custom web/offline-sw.js that races network against a 3.5-second timeout before falling back to cache:

// web/offline-sw.js
function networkFirst(request, timeoutMs) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('timeout')), timeoutMs);
    fetch(request)
      .then((response) => {
        if (response && response.ok) {
          caches.open(CACHE).then((cache) => cache.put(request, response.clone()));
        }
        resolve(response);
      })
      .catch(reject)
      .finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
  }).catch(() => caches.match(request));
}

Notice the .finally(() => clearTimeout(timer)) cleanup: without it, every fast network response leaves an orphan timer running until timeoutMs expires.

Benchmarking: Cloud CI vs. Local Verification Gate

Stage GitHub Actions (ubuntu-latest) Local Apple Silicon Gate Improvement
Python CLI Unit Tests (68 tests) 14.2s (with setup) 0.02s 710x faster
Dart Format + Analyze + 466 Flutter tests 118.0s 14.5s 8.1x faster
flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn 142.0s 14.8s 9.6x faster
firebase deploy --only hosting:board 34.0s 3.1s 11.0x faster
Total Wall-Clock Time ~5m 08s (plus SDK cache) ~32.4s ~9.5x faster, $0 CI cost

Table totals exclude the Flutter SDK download and Pub cache warm-up (~90s), which is what brings a full PR run to ~6.5 minutes.

Key Takeaways for Flutter & Firebase Engineers

  1. Keep CI YAML for PRs when budget allows, but make your local gate identical. A single local command (dart format -l 120 lib/ test/ && flutter analyze && python3 -m unittest discover -s tool -p '*_test.py' && flutter test) guarantees parity before firebase deploy.
  2. Use Firebase Hosting multi-site targets (hosting:board, hosting:board-staging). Mapping targets in .firebaserc lets you preview on staging or promote to live with --only hosting:board without touching sibling sites on the same GCP project.
  3. Never let one bad Firestore document take down a collection stream. Wrap per-document .fromJson() calls inside a helper that logs to dart:developer and skips the corrupted record.
  4. Test accessibility contrast and 44pt tap targets in flutter test, not in production. Running textContrastGuideline and androidTapTargetGuideline with GoogleFonts.config.allowRuntimeFetching = false catches neon text shadow contrast drops and 32pt icons in milliseconds.

The complete local release gate in one command:

dart format -l 120 lib/ test/ && \
  flutter analyze && \
  python3 -m unittest discover -s tool -p '*_test.py' && \
  flutter test && \
  flutter build web --release --no-web-resources-cdn && \
  firebase deploy --only hosting:board --project esra-life-os

articles.title: TypeScript `ReadonlyDeep<T>` Without a Library: Writing the Recursive Utility Type Once and Never Again
articles.description: Build a production-ready ReadonlyDeep utility type that makes nested object properties immutable at compile time without external dependencies.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript ReadonlyDeep<T> Without a Library: Writing the Recursive Utility Type Once and Never Again

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Why Built-In Readonly Isn't Enough

TypeScript's built-in Readonly<T> type applies immutability to top-level properties but stops there. Nested objects remain mutable. When a developer marks a configuration object as readonly and a teammate mutates a nested property three levels deep, the compiler stays silent. The bug appears in production.

Problem flow showing built-in Readonly allowing nested mutations

A recursive readonly type solves this. Every property at every depth becomes immutable. The compiler catches mutations before they ship.

Solution flow showing ReadonlyDeep preventing all mutations

Key Takeaways

  • TypeScript's Readonly<T> only protects top-level properties; nested objects remain mutable and cause silent bugs.
  • A recursive ReadonlyDeep<T> utility type applies immutability to all properties at every depth without runtime overhead.
  • The implementation requires handling primitives, functions, arrays, Maps, Sets, and circular references with conditional types.
  • Type-fest's version adds complexity for edge cases; a focused implementation works for most codebases in under 30 lines.
  • Compiler performance degrades past 10 nesting levels or 100+ properties; measure before applying to massive schemas.

Understanding the ReadonlyDeep Signature

The type signature needs to handle every TypeScript construct. Primitives like string, number, and boolean pass through unchanged. Functions preserve their signatures. Arrays become readonly arrays. Objects recurse into their properties.

Type hierarchy showing ReadonlyDeep branching by input type

The recursive case is where the type earns its place. For each property K in object T, the type constructs a new object with K mapped to ReadonlyDeep<T[K]>. The recursion stops when it hits a primitive or function.

TypeScript's conditional types make this possible. The pattern T extends Primitive ? T : ... lets the type branch based on structure. Each branch handles a different category.

The built-in Readonly<T> handles the shallow case. ReadonlyDeep<T> wraps it with recursion. The combination creates a type that descends through arbitrarily nested structures.

Building ReadonlyDeep: The Base Case and Recursive Logic

The implementation starts with a type alias for primitives. This includes string, number, boolean, symbol, bigint, undefined, and null. Functions count as primitives here because their internal structure does not require recursion.

type Primitive =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | symbol
  | bigint
  | undefined
  | null;

type ReadonlyDeep<T> = T extends Primitive
  ? T
  : T extends Function
  ? T
  : T extends (infer U)[]
  ? ReadonlyArray<ReadonlyDeep<U>>
  : {
      readonly [K in keyof T]: ReadonlyDeep<T[K]>;
    };

The first condition checks if T is a primitive. If so, the type returns T unchanged. The second condition handles functions. The third condition matches arrays using the infer pattern and wraps them in ReadonlyArray.

The final case handles objects. The mapped type iterates over every key K in T. Each property becomes readonly, and the value type becomes ReadonlyDeep<T[K]>. The recursion happens here.

This version works for most cases. A configuration object with nested arrays and objects becomes fully immutable:

interface Config {
  database: {
    host: string;
    port: number;
    credentials: {
      username: string;
      password: string;
    };
  };
  features: string[];
}

type ImmutableConfig = ReadonlyDeep<Config>;

const config: ImmutableConfig = {
  database: {
    host: "localhost",
    port: 5432,
    credentials: {
      username: "admin",
      password: "secret",
    },
  },
  features: ["caching", "logging"],
};

// All of these produce compile-time errors:
config.database.port = 3306; // Error: Cannot assign to 'port'
config.database.credentials.password = "newpass"; // Error
config.features.push("metrics"); // Error: Property 'push' does not exist
config.features[0] = "telemetry"; // Error: Index signature is readonly

The compiler blocks every mutation attempt. No runtime checks. No library dependency.

TypeScript error panel showing blocked mutations on deeply nested readonly properties

Handling Edge Cases: Functions, Maps, Sets, and Arrays

The basic implementation breaks down with Map and Set. These types have methods like set and add that mutate internal state. TypeScript's ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet types exist for this reason.

The extended version adds conditions for these collections:

type Primitive =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | symbol
  | bigint
  | undefined
  | null;

type ReadonlyDeep<T> = T extends Primitive
  ? T
  : T extends Function
  ? T
  : T extends Map<infer K, infer V>
  ? ReadonlyMap<K, ReadonlyDeep<V>>
  : T extends Set<infer U>
  ? ReadonlySet<ReadonlyDeep<U>>
  : T extends (infer U)[]
  ? ReadonlyArray<ReadonlyDeep<U>>
  : {
      readonly [K in keyof T]: ReadonlyDeep<T[K]>;
    };

The Map branch infers key and value types, wraps the value in ReadonlyDeep, and returns ReadonlyMap. The Set branch does the same with ReadonlySet. Both prevent mutations while preserving read operations.

Functions with properties require careful handling. A function can have properties attached to it, and those properties should become readonly:

interface Logger {
  (message: string): void;
  level: string;
}

type ReadonlyLogger = ReadonlyDeep<Logger>;

const logger: ReadonlyLogger = Object.assign(
  (message: string) => console.log(message),
  { level: "info" }
);

logger("test"); // Works
logger.level = "debug"; // Error: Cannot assign to 'level'

The function condition in the type needs to come after the primitive check but before the object recursion. This preserves the function signature while applying readonly to any attached properties.

Arrays of arrays require the recursion to work properly. The type string[][] becomes ReadonlyArray<ReadonlyArray<string>>. Each level of nesting applies both ReadonlyArray and ReadonlyDeep to the inner type.

For more on working with readonly collections, see ReadonlyMap and ReadonlySet in TypeScript.

ReadonlyDeep vs type-fest vs Manual Implementation

The type-fest library provides a ReadonlyDeep implementation with additional features. It handles classes, preserves function properties, and includes special cases for built-in types. The tradeoff is complexity.

Comparison of three ReadonlyDeep approaches

The custom implementation covers objects, arrays, functions, Maps, and Sets. This handles 95% of use cases in application code. Type-fest adds support for classes with private fields, WeakMaps, Promises, and other specialized types.

Here's the comparison on a complex type:

interface APISchema {
  users: Map<
    string,
    {
      profile: {
        name: string;
        tags: string[];
      };
      settings: Set<string>;
    }
  >;
  metadata: {
    version: number;
    handlers: Array<(data: unknown) => void>;
  };
}

// Custom implementation handles this correctly:
type ImmutableSchema = ReadonlyDeep<APISchema>;

// type-fest adds these guarantees:
// - Class instances preserve private field types
// - WeakMap and WeakSet get readonly versions
// - Promise values become readonly
// - Tuple types preserve length and ordering

For most codebases, the custom version works. The compiler errors guide you when edge cases appear. Adding type-fest as a dependency makes sense when you hit repeated gaps in coverage.

The maintenance burden differs. A custom utility type lives in the codebase and requires updates when TypeScript adds new built-in types. Type-fest tracks these changes and ships updates.

Teams building component libraries or TypeScript tooling benefit from type-fest's thoroughness. Application developers building features on a known stack rarely need that level of coverage.

For related patterns on partial immutability, see Partial, Required, and DeepPartial in TypeScript.

Real-World Use Cases: API Responses and Configuration Objects

API response types become safer with ReadonlyDeep. A response handler receives data from the network and should not modify it. The readonly constraint prevents accidental mutations that break caching or introduce race conditions.

interface UserResponse {
  user: {
    id: string;
    profile: {
      name: string;
      email: string;
      preferences: {
        theme: string;
        notifications: string[];
      };
    };
  };
  metadata: {
    timestamp: number;
    version: string;
  };
}

async function fetchUser(
  id: string
): Promise<ReadonlyDeep<UserResponse>> {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`);
  return response.json();
}

async function displayUser(id: string) {
  const data = await fetchUser(id);

  // All mutation attempts blocked:
  data.user.profile.name = "Modified"; // Error
  data.user.profile.preferences.notifications.push("email"); // Error
  data.metadata.timestamp = Date.now(); // Error

  // Reading works normally:
  console.log(data.user.profile.name);
  console.log(data.user.profile.preferences.theme);
}

Data flow showing readonly API response preventing mutations

Configuration objects gain the same protection. Application config loads once at startup and should never change. Making it readonly catches bugs where code tries to modify settings based on runtime conditions.

interface AppConfig {
  server: {
    port: number;
    host: string;
    ssl: {
      enabled: boolean;
      certPath: string;
    };
  };
  database: {
    connections: Array<{
      name: string;
      url: string;
      poolSize: number;
    }>;
  };
  features: Map<string, boolean>;
}

let config: ReadonlyDeep<AppConfig>;

function loadConfig(): ReadonlyDeep<AppConfig> {
  // Load from environment or config file
  return {
    server: {
      port: 3000,
      host: "0.0.0.0",
      ssl: {
        enabled: true,
        certPath: "/etc/ssl/cert.pem",
      },
    },
    database: {
      connections: [
        {
          name: "primary",
          url: "postgresql://localhost/db",
          poolSize: 10,
        },
      ],
    },
    features: new Map([
      ["caching", true],
      ["telemetry", false],
    ]),
  };
}

function initializeApp() {
  config = loadConfig();

  // Runtime modifications blocked:
  config.server.port = 4000; // Error
  config.database.connections[0].poolSize = 20; // Error
  config.features.set("logging", true); // Error
}

IDE tooltip showing readonly error when attempting to modify nested config property

Form validation schemas work well with readonly types. The schema defines structure and constraints. Validators read from it but should not modify it. See Custom Form Validators in TypeScript for validator patterns.

State management libraries benefit from readonly types. Redux state, Zustand stores, and React context values all gain safety when typed as ReadonlyDeep. The compiler prevents direct mutations and forces proper update patterns.

Performance Considerations and Compiler Limits

TypeScript's type checker has recursion limits. Deep nesting or large object types can hit these limits and cause compilation errors. The practical limit sits around 10 levels of nesting for complex types.

Type checking performance showing degradation with nesting depth

A type with 100 properties at 3 levels deep creates 100^3 = 1,000,000 type instantiations. The compiler caches these, but initial compilation takes time. Watch for slow type checking during development.

The workaround is to limit recursion depth. Add a depth parameter that decrements with each recursion:

type Primitive =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | symbol
  | bigint
  | undefined
  | null;

type ReadonlyDeep<T, Depth extends number = 10> = Depth extends 0
  ? Readonly<T>
  : T extends Primitive
  ? T
  : T extends Function
  ? T
  : T extends Map<infer K, infer V>
  ? ReadonlyMap<K, ReadonlyDeep<V, Prev<Depth>>>
  : T extends Set<infer U>
  ? ReadonlySet<ReadonlyDeep<U, Prev<Depth>>>
  : T extends (infer U)[]
  ? ReadonlyArray<ReadonlyDeep<U, Prev<Depth>>>
  : {
      readonly [K in keyof T]: ReadonlyDeep<T[K], Prev<Depth>>;
    };

type Prev<N extends number> = N extends 0
  ? 0
  : N extends 1
  ? 0
  : N extends 2
  ? 1
  : N extends 3
  ? 2
  : N extends 4
  ? 3
  : N extends 5
  ? 4
  : N extends 6
  ? 5
  : N extends 7
  ? 6
  : N extends 8
  ? 7
  : N extends 9
  ? 8
  : N extends 10
  ? 9
  : never;

This version stops recursing after 10 levels and falls back to shallow Readonly. The Prev helper decrements the depth counter. When depth reaches zero, recursion stops.

Measure compilation time with tsc --diagnostics. Look for the "Type checking time" metric. If it exceeds one second, investigate which types cause the slowness.

Large codebases should apply ReadonlyDeep selectively. Configuration objects, API responses, and constants benefit from it. Internal implementation types that change frequently create unnecessary compilation overhead.

The type system overhead is zero at runtime. ReadonlyDeep is purely a compile-time construct. The JavaScript output contains no traces of it.

Frequently Asked Questions

How does ReadonlyDeep differ from const assertions?

Const assertions make literal types as narrow as possible and add shallow readonly to objects. ReadonlyDeep applies deep immutability to existing type definitions. Use const assertions for inline objects and ReadonlyDeep for reusable types.

Can ReadonlyDeep handle circular references?

No. Circular type references cause infinite recursion in TypeScript's type checker. The depth-limited version prevents compiler hangs but does not make circular structures readonly. Avoid circular references or use shallow Readonly for those cases.

Does ReadonlyDeep work with generics?

Yes. Pass generic types to ReadonlyDeep like any other type. The recursion applies to whatever type the generic resolves to at usage time.

Will ReadonlyDeep prevent all runtime mutations?

No. TypeScript types disappear at runtime. ReadonlyDeep provides compile-time safety only. Use Object.freeze() for runtime immutability or combine both approaches for defense in depth.

Should every type use ReadonlyDeep by default?

No. Apply it to data that should not change: configuration, API responses, constants. Internal implementation types that undergo frequent mutations benefit from normal mutability. Overuse creates friction without safety gains.

Write It Once, Use It Forever

The ReadonlyDeep<T> utility type solves the nested mutability problem that built-in Readonly<T> leaves open. Thirty lines of code eliminate an entire class of bugs. The compiler catches mutations at every depth before they reach production.

The implementation handles objects, arrays, functions, Maps, and Sets. Edge cases exist but rarely matter in application code. Teams that need comprehensive coverage can reach for type-fest. Teams building features on standard types can write this once and never think about it again.

Configuration objects and API responses gain immediate safety benefits. State management becomes more predictable. The type system enforces immutability contracts that previously existed only in documentation.

Compilation time matters for large schemas. Measure performance and limit recursion depth when needed. The tradeoff between safety and build speed is concrete and measurable.

Adding this utility type to a codebase takes five minutes and prevents mutations that take hours to debug.

articles.title: Next.js 16 updateTag vs revalidateTag: What Changed
articles.description: Next.js 16 deprecated revalidateTag's single-argument call and added updateTag. What the new profile argument changes, plus a copy-paste cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
Your team upgrades to Next.js 16, the build passes, and nothing in the diff touches caching. A week later, publishing a blog post starts taking noticeably longer — not to save, but for the next reader to see it. Somewhere in a Server Action sits a line nobody touched: revalidateTag('posts'). It still runs. It just does something different now.

That line used to mark the posts tag stale and move on — the next visitor got the old page instantly while Next.js refreshed it in the background. In Next.js 16, the same one-argument call is deprecated, and its behavior changed to match an immediate, blocking cache miss: the next request to anything tagged posts now waits for fresh data before it renders.
