Day 26 of 30 Days of Search.

TL;DR

You can build much more than a search interface with Valyu APIs. These ten apps turn retrieved evidence into biomedical research, consulting reports, investment analysis, geopolitical maps, patent discovery, pharmaceutical content reviews, and scientific research briefs. Each profile below includes what the app does, its stack, Valyu's role, a repository link, a live app link, and a screenshot.

One distinction matters: not all ten currently call Search API directly for their main workflow. Some use Search to retrieve evidence for application-owned reasoning. Others use DeepResearch to run a research task and return a cited report. This collection shows both patterns.

What can you build with Valyu Search API and DeepResearch?

A researcher does not need another list of links. They need to compare clinical evidence. A fund manager needs to find the weakness in a thesis. A consultant needs a research brief they can turn into a client discussion.

That is the starting point for these apps: a specific job, with search and research underneath it.

The Valyu Search API returns results your application can reason over. DeepResearch handles a longer investigation and returns research output. The interface, review steps, and next action are where each product becomes different.

App The job it helps with Valyu's role in the current app
Bio Research biomedical questions and life sciences workflows DeepResearch workflows and cited reports
Consult Ralph Prepare company, market, and competitive research DeepResearch with downloadable deliverables
Finance Produce financial research briefs and investment memos DeepResearch workflows and report generation
Global Threat Map Explore geopolitical events and actor intelligence News and entity Search, plus DeepResearch dossiers
Polyseer Investigate a Polymarket or Kalshi market DeepResearch grounded in the market's question and rules
Patents Find patent documents and investigate prior art Search across USPTO and EPO patent sources
OpenWhales Investigate institutional holdings and insider activity SEC and financial Search tools
OpenMLR Pre-check pharmaceutical promotional claims Claim-specific Search, with specialist DeepResearch lanes
Devil's Advocate Challenge an investment thesis against a mandate Sourced research, including DeepResearch for attachment-backed analysis
ARC-AGI-N Discover open research problems and plan an attempt Web and academic Search, plus DeepResearch plans

The screenshots show the hosted interfaces as captured on October 26, 2026. Built-in examples illustrate the products, not independently validated research findings. Some actions require sign-in and credits.

1. Bio: turn a biomedical question into a research brief

Bio helps researchers investigate questions that span scientific papers, clinical trials, drug labels, and patents. Suppose you are comparing approaches to CAR-T treatment for lupus: choose a competitive-landscape workflow, specify the research scope, then review a cited report before deciding which programmes need closer reading. Valyu DeepResearch runs the investigation across biomedical and web sources. Bio adds the life sciences workflow browser, research-depth controls, report history, and deliverables, turning a broad question into material a research team can inspect rather than an unsupported answer.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Drizzle, and SQLite or Supabase.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/bio

Live app: https://bio.valyu.ai

Bio organises research around life sciences jobs. Its output supports research, not clinical diagnosis or treatment decisions.

2. Consult Ralph: start a consulting engagement with a sourced brief

Consult Ralph helps consultants prepare company due diligence, market analysis, competitive intelligence, and industry research. For example, a consultant assessing a market-entry opportunity can name the market, add the client's context and specific questions, and request a brief with supporting files. Valyu DeepResearch performs the research and generates the requested deliverables. The app packages that work into a consulting-specific form and results view, so the next step is reviewing assumptions and shaping a client recommendation, not copying scattered search results into a document.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and valyu-js.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/consultralph

Live app: https://consultralph.com

The brief starts with the consulting question and client context; the deliverables support the work that follows.

3. Finance: build research around the investment workflow

Finance helps analysts move from a company or investment question to a cited financial research report. An analyst preparing for an investment committee meeting can start with a company profile or memo workflow, set the scope, and inspect the supporting sources before taking a position to the team. The current app uses Valyu DeepResearch and a financial-services workflow catalogue, rather than making the user orchestrate individual searches. Finance provides the report interface, research history, and controls for charts, code execution, and deliverables.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Drizzle, and SQLite or Supabase.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/finance

Live app: https://finance.valyu.ai

Finance turns a financial research question into a reviewable report. It does not execute trades.

4. Global Threat Map: give geopolitical research a geographic interface

Global Threat Map puts security events, geographic context, and actor research on an interactive globe. An analyst investigating a regional disruption can explore the map, narrow the event feed, and investigate a relevant organisation before preparing a briefing. Valyu Search supplies news and entity-background retrieval; DeepResearch supports longer intelligence dossiers. Mapbox handles the geographic interface and map layers. That separation matters: Valyu supplies research evidence, not every flight, fire, or earthquake marker displayed by the app.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Mapbox GL JS, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and valyu-js.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/globalthreatmap

Live app: https://globalthreatmap.up.railway.app

The captured map is public; its event feed is sign-in gated. A marker is a starting point for investigation, not a verified threat assessment.

5. Polyseer: research the question behind a prediction-market price

Polyseer helps users investigate markets on Polymarket and Kalshi. Paste a market URL, and the app reads the question, prices, closing date, and resolution rules before starting research. Someone examining a central-bank decision market can compare the resulting estimated probability, supporting evidence, and risks against the market price, then decide whether the apparent disagreement deserves more investigation. Valyu DeepResearch runs that investigation and returns structured forecasting output and supporting files. Polyseer supplies the market context and the interface for following the research.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and Polymarket/Kalshi API integrations.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/Polyseer

Live app: https://polyseer.xyz

A research estimate can be wrong. Polyseer is not a guarantee of a forecasting edge or a profitable trade.

6. Patents: move from an invention description to documents worth reading

Patents, branded PatentAI in the interface, helps builders and researchers investigate patent documents in natural language. A hardware team exploring solid-state batteries can describe the mechanism, narrow the jurisdiction, and inspect related patent records and drawings before deciding what to take to a patent professional. Valyu Search retrieves USPTO and EPO patent material; the app adds conversational investigation, patent-identity handling, and analysis tools. The useful outcome is a better set of documents and questions, not an automated declaration that an invention is patentable or safe to commercialise.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK, valyu-js, Recharts, and Daytona.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/patents

Live app: https://patents.valyu.ai

Use retrieved patent documents to guide further investigation. Prior-art and freedom-to-operate conclusions require qualified review.

7. OpenWhales: follow institutional and insider disclosures

OpenWhales helps investors investigate what institutions, activist investors, and corporate insiders have disclosed in SEC filings. Search a ticker such as NVDA or an investor's name to explore holdings, transactions, and a sourced narrative, then open the filings behind an interesting change. Valyu's SEC Search tools supply the filing evidence, with additional financial, economic, and company-research tools available for follow-up questions. OpenWhales turns that retrieval into holdings tables, transaction views, and conversational analysis, with Redis caching for repeat requests.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK, @valyu/ai-sdk, Redis, and Zustand.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/openwhales

Live app: https://open-whales.com

A disclosure tells you what was reported for a particular date or period. It is not a live view of an investor's complete portfolio or intentions.

8. OpenMLR: check pharmaceutical claims against retrieved evidence

OpenMLR is a medical, legal, and regulatory pre-check for pharmaceutical promotional content. A reviewer can paste a draft asset containing a comparative efficacy claim, inspect the evidence attached to each finding, and decide whether to accept it, request a revision, or reject it. Valyu Search retrieves claim-specific material from sources such as drug labels, PubMed, and clinical trials, while specialist checks can run through DeepResearch. The app adds claim extraction, review decisions, an audit trail, and a reusable claims library. Human reviewers remain responsible for the determination.

Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, valyu-js, Zod, Streamdown, and optional PostgreSQL.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/openmlr

Live app: https://openmlr.up.railway.app

This is the app's preloaded sample, not a review performed for this article or a medical or regulatory endorsement of its findings.

9. Devil's Advocate: challenge an investment thesis before committee

Devil's Advocate helps fund managers stress-test investment memos against evidence and their own mandate. Write a stock, fund, or private-company thesis, then examine objections from bull, bear, and house-view review roles. The next step is addressing the objections or revising the memo before moving it towards investment committee review. Valyu supplies sourced research, including DeepResearch for attachment-backed investigations. The app adds the adversarial review process, per-manager rules, memo states, and PDF export, making the research part of an explicit decision workflow rather than another detached report.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK, TipTap, Drizzle, SQLite, and Playwright.

Repository: https://github.com/unicodeveloper/devilsadvocate

Live app: https://devilsadvocate.up.railway.app

The screenshot shows read-only examples. An app-level approval is a workflow state, not an investment recommendation.

10. ARC-AGI-N: find a research problem and a place to start

ARC-AGI-N helps people discover open questions in mathematics and science, read the supporting literature, and prepare an agent-ready research brief. Someone interested in climate science can search for problems, inspect the cited sources, choose a tractable starting question, and request a deeper research plan. Valyu Search powers discovery across web and academic material; DeepResearch produces longer plans. The app adds a browsable globe, structured problem cards, and copyable research prompts. It helps choose the next investigation, without claiming to prove that a question remains unsolved.

Stack: Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK, Mapbox GL JS, valyu-js, and KaTeX.

Repository: https://github.com/yorkeccak/arc-agi-n

Live app: https://arc-agi-n.com

ARC-AGI-N is an independent project, not an official ARC Prize benchmark. Check recent primary literature before claiming a problem is still open.

What these ten apps have in common

The differentiator is not that each app has a search box. It is what happens after retrieval: a document gets reviewed, a thesis gets challenged, a market question gets investigated, or a research problem becomes a concrete next step.

If you are building something similar, start with the user's job and work backwards:

  1. Define the decision or output. A shortlist, research brief, evidence check, or investment memo needs a different interface.
  2. Choose Search or DeepResearch deliberately. Use Search when your application controls retrieval and reasoning. Use DeepResearch when you want a completed investigation and cited output.
  3. Keep the evidence visible. Preserve source links, dates, and relevant passages so someone can check the interpretation.
  4. Make the next action explicit. Open the filing, read the paper, revise the claim, or request a deeper investigation.

You can study the repositories above, check their licences and setup requirements, and adapt the relevant pattern to your own application. For a smaller starting point, see the Valyu quickstart and Vercel AI SDK integration.

Frequently asked questions

Are all ten apps built directly on Valyu Search API?

No. Patents and OpenWhales expose clear application-owned Search patterns. Bio, Finance, Consult Ralph, and Polyseer currently use DeepResearch for their main research workflows. Global Threat Map, OpenMLR, and ARC-AGI-N combine search and longer research. Devil's Advocate uses Valyu research within its memo-review process. Study the current implementation rather than assuming every app follows the same architecture.

Can I run these applications myself?

The repositories are public, and the projects document deployment or local setup. Check each repository's licence, environment variables, required services, and source access before reusing it. Self-hosting the interface does not make API calls free; check current Valyu pricing.

Were the screenshots generated from new paid research runs?

No. They were captured from the hosted interfaces and a public built-in sample review. No new paid research task was launched to prepare this article. Screenshots demonstrate the product interface, not research accuracy, production traffic, or a measured performance benchmark.

Build your next research app

Pick one job from this collection and give your agent the evidence it needs to do it. Start with the API documentation, get a key at platform.valyu.ai, and keep the sources attached to the result.

The search is the beginning. The useful application is what you build around it.

articles.title: Python 3.14's concurrent.interpreters module turns a 3.6-second GIL bottleneck into 0.9 seconds
articles.description: I measured Python 3.14's new subinterpreters against threads and processes: 3.6s of GIL contention dropped to 0.9s, but a single interpreter flatly refuses a second concurrent thread.
articles.body_html:
A CPU-bound Python job split across four threads took 3.6 seconds on my machine. The same job split across four of Python 3.14's new subinterpreters took 0.9 seconds, roughly what one thread alone takes to do a quarter of the work. That part matched what I expected from the PEP. What I did not expect was that asking one of those subinterpreters to run two things at once does not slow it down. It refuses outright.

concurrent.interpreters is new in the standard library as of Python 3.14, released on 7 October 2026. Subinterpreters themselves are not new - they have existed in the C API since Python 1.5 and CPython has used them internally for years - but PEP 734 is what makes them usable from ordinary Python code, with no C extension required. Each subinterpreter gets its own Global Interpreter Lock, which is the part worth testing: it is the thing that is supposed to let CPU-bound Python code actually use more than one core without reaching for multiprocessing.

I tested it against a CPU-bound workload (counting primes below 400,000, a plain Python double loop with no C extensions to hide behind), compared against threads, processes, and a single thread, three runs each, inside a python:3.14-slim container with four cores available.

The headline number

approach time for 4x the work
single thread (1x unit, for reference) 0.77 - 0.80s
4 OS threads, classic GIL 3.51 - 3.70s
4 subinterpreters (new in 3.14) 0.89 - 0.98s
4 processes (multiprocessing) 0.95 - 1.30s

Four threads doing four units of CPU-bound work took more than four times as long as one thread doing one unit - 3.6s against roughly 0.8s, which is actually a bit worse than the 3.2s you'd get from perfect serialisation, because the GIL has to keep stopping one thread to let another run. Four subinterpreters doing the same four units took about 0.9s: close enough to the single-unit baseline that the extra three units of work were, for practical purposes, free. That is real parallelism, not a scheduling trick, and it lands in the same place multiprocessing already does.

What it refuses: one thread per interpreter, not shared

The PEP's selling point is that each interpreter has its own GIL. I wanted to see what happens when two threads try to use one interpreter's GIL at the same time, expecting it to behave like classic Python: both threads run, the shared GIL makes them take turns.

That is not what happened. A single Interpreter object only tolerates one caller. A second concurrent call doesn't queue, and it doesn't share time with the first - it is rejected immediately:

Exception in thread Thread-2 (_call):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/local/lib/python3.14/concurrent/interpreters/__init__.py", line 226, in _call
    res, excinfo = _interpreters.call(self._id, callable, args, kwargs, restrict=True)
concurrent.interpreters.InterpreterError: interpreter already running

I confirmed the shape of this with three variants of the same interpreter, run in sequence:

scenario time outcome
one call 0.84s fine
two sequential calls, same interpreter 1.63s fine, roughly 2x
two concurrent calls, same interpreter 0.84s wall-clock second call raises InterpreterError

interpreters.create() is documented as returning "a new (idle) Python interpreter", and that word is accurate: idle or running, nothing in between. If you want N things running at once, you need N interpreters, one each. A thread pool aimed at a single shared interpreter - the pattern every ThreadPoolExecutor tutorial uses with regular threads - does not translate. You get one interpreter's worth of work and an exception, not graceful serialisation.

The opposite number: interpreters are not obviously cheaper to start than processes

The other assumption I walked in with was that subinterpreters, being lighter than OS processes, would be cheap to spin up. I measured the cost of creating four workers and giving each one some real state (a 200,000-element list), steady state after the first warm-up run:

approach create + populate, 4 workers
fork (Python 3.13's Linux default) 0.037 - 0.038s
forkserver (Python 3.14's Linux default) 0.057 - 0.065s
4 subinterpreters 0.076 - 0.078s

Creating four subinterpreters and running a small amount of code in each took about twice as long as a classic fork-based process pool, and somewhat longer than the new forkserver default too. None of this matters once the work inside each worker takes more than a few milliseconds - the 3.6s-versus-0.9s number above swallows an 80-millisecond setup cost without noticing. But it means "subinterpreters are lighter than processes" is not something I could verify at creation time; the saving, where it exists, is in not forking a second copy of the process's address space, not in any faster start.

That forkserver row was an accident. I wrote a timing script that called multiprocessing.Process(...).start() directly from the module's top level, the way plenty of tutorial code still does, and it crashed:

RuntimeError:
        An attempt has been made to start a new process before the
        current process has finished its bootstrapping phase.

Checking multiprocessing.get_start_method() explained it: Python 3.14 changed the default start method on Linux from fork to forkserver. Python 3.13 reports fork; 3.14 reports forkserver. forkserver re-imports your module in the child, which is exactly the thing if __name__ == "__main__": exists to guard against, and which fork never required you to bother with. Every piece of multiprocessing code I'd written without that guard over the years happened to work by accident, on Linux, until this release. It's a one-line fix, but it is a real break, and it landed in the same release that gives you an alternative that doesn't have this problem at all.

What it costs: closing an interpreter doesn't give the memory back

I ran four rounds of "create four interpreters, give each a 200,000-element list, close them", watching my own process's RSS the whole time:

round 1: 16920 -> 55648 KB
round 2: 55648 -> 57140 KB
round 3: 57140 -> 59476 KB
round 4: 59476 -> 61096 KB

.close() does finalise the interpreter - a destroyed interpreter can't be called again, and I checked that it raises if you try - but the process's resident memory never drops back to where it started. It flattens out (each later round adds less than the first) rather than growing without bound, which looks like CPython's allocator holding onto freed arenas rather than a genuine leak, but I didn't chase that further. If you're planning to cycle through many short-lived interpreters inside one long-running process, budget for that memory to stay resident, not to be returned to the OS the way a finished process's memory is.

What's actually shareable between interpreters

Subinterpreters don't share objects by default - that is the entire point, it's what lets them skip the GIL - so most interesting values need to cross a boundary. is_shareable() gives a yes/no answer per type:

int              -> True
str              -> True
bytes            -> True
None             -> True
bool             -> True
tuple of ints    -> True
float            -> True
list             -> False
dict             -> False

Passing a threading.Lock as an argument to Interpreter.call() fails immediately, with the repr of the offending object right there in the message:

NotShareableError: (<unlocked _thread.lock object at 0x7f61b8b5add0>,) does not support cross-interpreter data

An ordinary custom class instance fails the same way, with a flatter message:

NotShareableError: object does not support cross-interpreter data

But the cross-interpreter Queue that the same module provides does not enforce this. I put a plain custom-class instance onto a queue and it went through without complaint, and came back out as a distinct, working object with the same attribute values - the queue silently pickles and unpickles it:

q = interpreters.create_queue()
q.put(Thing())          # no error
received = q.get()
# received is not the original object, but received.value is unchanged

So "not shareable" is enforced differently depending on how the object crosses over. A direct argument to call() is checked against the strict shareable-types list and rejected on the spot. The same object dropped into a Queue gets the softer treatment the docs describe for put(): pickled going in, unpickled coming out as a new, unrelated object. If your code passes data between interpreters by argument, moving it to a queue instead buys you a much larger set of types - at the cost of identity and, for anything mutable, of staying in sync with the original.

What I got wrong on the way

My first attempt at the shareability tests put several checks in one script with no if __name__ == "__main__": guard, calling interp.call() with a mix of shareable and non-shareable arguments one after another. Running it printed every result twice, and the second copy sometimes disagreed with the first about which error got raised. My best explanation, which I didn't fully verify, is that call()'s documented pickle fallback needs to resolve names against the target interpreter's own __main__, and since that interpreter had never run my module, resolving anything defined at module level meant running the whole module there first - silently re-executing my test file a second time, inside the subinterpreter, with its own fresh state. Splitting each check into its own small script with a proper __main__ guard made every result reproducible, which is what's reported above. I'd treat any subinterpreter test that imports a lot of top-level code as suspect until it survives being run twice.

Run it yourself

This needs Python 3.14 and four-ish cores to see the gap clearly. I ran it in Docker because that's the fastest way to get an exact version:

docker pull python:3.14-slim

The core benchmark:

# bench.py
import time, threading, sys

def cpu_work(n):
    count = 0
    for i in range(2, n):
        is_prime = True
        for d in range(2, int(i ** 0.5) + 1):
            if i % d == 0:
                is_prime = False
                break
        if is_prime:
            count += 1
    return count

def run_threads(n, workers):
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=cpu_work, args=(n,)) for _ in range(workers)]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"threads={workers}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.3f}s")

def run_interpreters(n, workers):
    import concurrent.interpreters as interpreters
    interps = [interpreters.create() for _ in range(workers)]
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    threads = [i.call_in_thread(cpu_work, n) for i in interps]
    for t in threads: t.join()
    print(f"interpreters={workers}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:.3f}s")
    for i in interps: i.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mode, n, workers = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), int(sys.argv[3])
    {"threads": run_threads, "interpreters": run_interpreters}[mode](n, workers)

docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w python:3.14-slim python3 bench.py threads 400000 4
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w python:3.14-slim python3 bench.py interpreters 400000 4

And the refusal, which needs no setup at all:

docker run --rm python:3.14-slim python3 -c "
import concurrent.interpreters as interpreters
i = interpreters.create()
t1 = i.call_in_thread(lambda: __import__('time').sleep(1))
t2 = i.call_in_thread(lambda: __import__('time').sleep(1))
t1.join(); t2.join()
"

What to do with this

If you have a CPU-bound Python workload that multiprocessing already parallelises well, subinterpreters aren't an obvious upgrade yet: on this release they start up slower than a plain fork and about the same as forkserver, and you still need one interpreter per concurrent task, with no pooling against a single interpreter. Where they're worth trying now is the code that currently reaches for a thread, because threading is simpler to wire up than multiprocessing, and then quietly gets nothing from the GIL: swap the Thread for an Interpreter.call_in_thread, and check your data either fits the shareable-types list or is willing to cross as a pickled copy through a Queue. And if you have multiprocessing code anywhere that starts a Process without an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, fix that first - 3.14 will find it on Linux even if nothing else in this post applies to you.

articles.title: How I finally understood the Liskov Substitution Principle
articles.description: The Intro   Halfway through SOLID! We are at the L, the one with the scary name: the Liskov...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Halfway through SOLID! We are at the L, the one with the scary name: the Liskov Substitution Principle.

If the previous two felt like common sense with fancy labels, this one is the first that usually catches people off guard. I have shipped the exact bug we are about to write. More than once. 🙃

The What

The original definition is a math paper from 1987 and reads like one:

If S is a subtype of T, then objects of type T may be replaced with objects of type S without altering any of the desirable properties of the program.

Let me translate: if your code works with the parent, it must also work with any child, without surprises. No instanceof checks, no "oh but not that one".

The usual example is squares and rectangles. I have never once had a square in production, so let's do something you will actually run into: payments and refunds.

The How

Our store accepts a few ways to pay. Each one can charge and refund:

// src/payment-method.ts
export abstract class PaymentMethod {
  abstract charge(amount: number): Promise<void>
  abstract refund(amount: number): Promise<void>
}

// src/card-payment.ts
import { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class CardPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 refunded $${amount}`)
  }
}

// src/paypal-payment.ts
import { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class PaypalPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🅿️ charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🅿️ refunded $${amount}`)
  }
}

And the part that uses them never cares which one it got:

// src/refund-service.ts
import type { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

interface Order {
  id: string
  total: number
  paidWith: PaymentMethod
}

export class RefundService {
  async refundAll(orders: Order[]) {
    for (const order of orders) {
      await order.paidWith.refund(order.total)
      console.log(`✅ order ${order.id} refunded`)
    }
  }
}

Beautiful. Substitutable. Barbara Liskov would be proud.

Then product adds gift cards. Gift cards can be charged, obviously. But legal says gift cards can't be refunded to cash. So we write the "obvious" thing:

// src/gift-card-payment.ts
import { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class GiftCardPayment extends PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🎁 charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund() {
    throw new Error('Gift cards cannot be refunded')
  }
}

It compiles. TypeScript is happy. The PR gets approved. 🚢

Three weeks later a product gets recalled and support runs the "refund everyone who bought it" script:

// src/main.ts
import { RefundService } from './refund-service.js'
import { CardPayment } from './card-payment.js'
import { GiftCardPayment } from './gift-card-payment.js'

const orders = [
  { id: 'A1', total: 40, paidWith: new CardPayment() },
  { id: 'A2', total: 25, paidWith: new GiftCardPayment() },
  { id: 'A3', total: 60, paidWith: new CardPayment() },
]

await new RefundService().refundAll(orders)

Output:

💳 refunded $40
✅ order A1 refunded
Error: Gift cards cannot be refunded

Order A1 refunded. Order A2 blew up. Order A3? Never happened. Customer A3 is now writing a one-star review.

That's a Liskov violation. RefundService was written against PaymentMethod, and the contract of PaymentMethod says "I can refund". GiftCardPayment said it was a PaymentMethod and then broke the promise at runtime.

The usual "fix" makes it worse:

if (order.paidWith instanceof GiftCardPayment) continue

Now RefundService knows about gift cards. Tomorrow it has to know about store credit. Then crypto. The whole point of the base class was to not know.

Step 1: stop lying in the type

The real problem is that the parent promised something not every child can keep. So let's make the promise smaller:

// src/payment-method.ts
export interface PaymentMethod {
  charge(amount: number): Promise<void>
}

export interface Refundable {
  refund(amount: number): Promise<void>
}

(Yes, we swapped the abstract class for interfaces. There was no shared code in the base anyway.)

Step 2: each method tells the truth 

// src/card-payment.ts
import type { PaymentMethod, Refundable } from './payment-method.js'

export class CardPayment implements PaymentMethod, Refundable {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  }

  async refund(amount: number) {
    console.log(`💳 refunded $${amount}`)
  }
}

// src/gift-card-payment.ts
import type { PaymentMethod } from './payment-method.js'

export class GiftCardPayment implements PaymentMethod {
  async charge(amount: number) {
    console.log(`🎁 charged $${amount}`)
  }
}

No refund() on the gift card. No throw. It just doesn't claim to be something it isn't.

Step 3: ask for exactly what you need 

// src/refund-service.ts
import type { Refundable } from './payment-method.js'

interface RefundableOrder {
  id: string
  total: number
  paidWith: Refundable
}

export class RefundService {
  async refundAll(orders: RefundableOrder[]) {
    for (const order of orders) {
      await order.paidWith.refund(order.total)
      console.log(`✅ order ${order.id} refunded`)
    }
  }
}

And now the best part. Go back to main.ts and try to pass a gift card order into refundAll():

Type 'GiftCardPayment' is not assignable to type 'Refundable'.
  Property 'refund' is missing in type 'GiftCardPayment'.

The compiler caught it. At build time. Not at 2 PM on recall day.

Whoever writes the refund script now has to decide up front what to do with gift card orders (issue store credit, email the customer, whatever). The decision moved from "a crash in a loop" to "a red squiggle in the editor".

The Why

Let's be explicit about the lesson, because it is subtle:

  • Inheritance is a promise, not a shortcut. "GiftCard is a PaymentMethod" sounded right in English. In code, it meant "GiftCard can do everything PaymentMethod can do", and that was false.
  • A method that throws NotSupported is a red flag. If a child has to disable a parent's method, the parent's contract is too big. Shrink it.
  • Callers depend on the smallest thing they need. RefundService needs refunds, so it asks for Refundable. Not PaymentMethod. Not CardPayment.
  • The type system becomes your QA. Every wrong combination fails to compile instead of failing in production.

If you remember one sentence: a subclass may do more than its parent, never less.

The Goodbye

Did you notice that fixing the L made us split one fat interface into two thin ones? That's not a coincidence. That's the I (Interface Segregation) knocking on the door, and it's up next.

Go search your codebase for throw new Error('not supported'). I'll wait. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: Your Form Says “Submitted”. So Where Did the Lead Go?
articles.description: Lead tracking should tell you what happens after someone fills out a form on your website. But what...
articles.body_html:
Lead tracking should tell you what happens after someone fills out a form on your website. But what happens when a visitor sees a confirmation message, your analytics records a conversion, and the lead never appears in your CRM?

For B2B SaaS marketing teams, this gap can create a serious blind spot. A campaign may appear to generate leads, yet sales sees fewer contacts than expected. Marketing starts checking campaign performance, sales questions the lead numbers, and someone eventually has to investigate the website, form integration, and CRM.

The tricky part is that the form can appear to work perfectly. The visitor submits their details, the page displays a success message, and an analytics event fires. None of those signals proves that the CRM received and saved the lead.

Reliable lead tracking depends on the full journey from the first form interaction to the contact record in your CRM. Every step needs to pass the right information to the next one, with enough visibility to catch errors before they affect reporting or sales follow-up.

In this guide, we'll look at where leads can disappear, how to trace a submission through the systems involved, and what B2B SaaS teams can do to make their tracking more reliable.

TL;DR

If a website form shows a successful submission but the lead never reaches your CRM, check the entire form-to-CRM process, not just the confirmation message or analytics event. The problem may come from a failed API request, a broken integration, field mapping errors, validation rules, duplicate handling, or a CRM workflow that rejects or changes the record.

Start with one test submission and follow it through each stage:

  1. Confirm that the website receives the form data.
  2. Check whether the form sends the data to the correct integration or endpoint.
  3. Review integration logs and API responses for errors.
  4. Verify that the CRM creates the contact or lead record.
  5. Check field mappings, duplicate rules, assignment settings, and automation.
  6. Compare form submissions with CRM records and analytics conversions to find gaps.

Good lead tracking gives marketing and sales a clearer picture of what actually happened. It also makes problems easier to diagnose before missing leads turn into missed opportunities.

Why Lead Tracking Can Fail Even When a Form Submission Succeeds

A success message usually confirms that the website has completed a specific step. Depending on how the form is built, it may mean the browser accepted the submission, the server received the request, or a form service returned a successful response.

That message does not always confirm that the CRM saved a new lead.

Consider a visitor who fills out a demo request form. The website displays a confirmation message, and Google Analytics records a conversion. However, the integration that sends the visitor's details to the CRM encounters an error. Marketing counts the conversion, but sales never receives the contact.

From the visitor's perspective, everything worked. From the business's perspective, the lead journey stopped before it reached the sales team.

Each System Confirms a Different Part of the Journey

A typical lead journey may involve several separate systems:

  • Website form: Collects the visitor's name, email address, company, and other details.
  • Form handler or backend: Receives the submission and processes the data.
  • Integration or API: Transfers the lead information to another system.
  • CRM: Creates or updates the contact or lead record.
  • Analytics and attribution tools: Record conversion activity and campaign details.

Some websites use a form platform that handles several of these steps. Others rely on custom code, automation tools, webhooks, or multiple integrations. The exact setup changes, but the same principle applies: a successful step does not guarantee that every later step succeeded.

How Lead Tracking Gaps Affect Marketing and Sales

Missing leads can distort campaign reports, delay sales follow-up, and make a successful campaign look weaker than it really is. The reverse can happen, too: analytics may count repeat submissions or conversions that never become usable CRM records.

Without reliable lead tracking, teams may struggle to answer basic questions. How many people requested a demo? Which campaigns generated contacts that sales could actually follow up with? Did a drop in leads come from campaign performance or a technical failure?

Before changing ad budgets or rewriting a landing page, make sure the systems handling the leads are reporting what actually happened.

The Most Common Places a Lead Can Disappear

When a lead fails to reach the CRM, the cause is often somewhere in the handoff between systems. Start by checking the following areas, then use logs and test submissions to narrow down the exact failure point.

1. Lead Tracking Failures in Form Integrations

A form may collect the visitor's details correctly while the next request fails. The integration might use an expired access token, an incorrect endpoint, a missing permission, or a request format that the receiving service does not accept.

For example, a CRM API may reject a request because a required field is missing. If the website still shows a generic success message, the visitor may never know that the lead was not saved.

Check the integration logs, request status, and error response where available. A successful browser interaction alone is not enough to confirm that the CRM received the data.

2. Field Mapping or Validation Rules Reject the Lead

Even when a request reaches the CRM, the data may not match the fields or rules expected by the system. A form might send a company name under the wrong field, use an unexpected date format, or leave a required CRM field empty.

Validation rules can also block a record. For example, the CRM may require a lead source, a valid email address, or a value from a predefined list. If the integration sends an unsupported value, the CRM may reject the request or leave the record incomplete.

Compare the form fields with their destination CRM fields, and check whether the integration transforms values before sending them. Pay attention to recently changed forms, CRM fields, and validation rules, since a small configuration change can interrupt the flow.

3. Duplicate Rules Prevent a New Lead From Being Created

A missing lead isn't always a lost submission. Some CRMs detect an existing contact or lead and block a new record from being created.

This can happen when someone submits a demo request using an email address already in the CRM. Depending on the duplicate rules, the system may reject the new record, update an existing contact, or flag the submission for review. The behavior varies by CRM configuration.

Check the duplicate handling rules and search for the submitted email address across both contacts and leads. The person may already exist, even if the sales team doesn't see a new lead in the expected view.

For example, Salesforce documents cases where duplicate rules prevent website form submissions from creating new lead records.

<Cite refs={["turn878168search0","turn878168search2"]} />

4. CRM Workflows Change or Redirect the Record

Sometimes the CRM receives the submission, but the lead ends up somewhere the team isn't looking.

Assignment rules may send it to another sales representative. Automation may change its status, associate it with an existing contact, or move it into a different queue. Filters and permissions can also make a record difficult to find.

Search the CRM using the email address from your test submission, then check the record's creation time, owner, status, and activity history. Review any automation triggered when a new lead arrives.

If the record exists but doesn't appear in the expected dashboard or lead list, investigate the CRM's views, filters, and assignment rules before changing the website integration.

5. Analytics Counts a Conversion That the CRM Never Receives

Analytics and CRM records measure different things. An analytics event can fire when a visitor clicks a submit button or reaches a confirmation page, even if the integration fails later.

This can inflate reported conversions and make campaign performance difficult to assess. A campaign might appear to generate plenty of leads while sales receives fewer contacts than expected.

Review the event configuration to understand exactly what triggers a conversion. Where possible, track confirmed submission success separately from the initial button click, and compare those events with actual CRM records.

Be careful with the numbers: one person may submit a form more than once, and a CRM may update an existing contact without creating a new lead. Those cases can explain differences between the totals without indicating a technical failure.

How to Fix Lead Tracking Issues From Form to CRM

Once you understand the possible failure points, the next step is to follow a test submission through the actual systems. This helps you identify where the data stops moving, instead of guessing which tool is responsible.

Step 1: Submit a Test Lead

Use a controlled test with a unique email address and realistic values for the required fields. Record the time of submission, the page URL, and the information entered.

If the form captures campaign details, check whether the relevant UTM parameters or hidden fields are included. Avoid using real customer information in test records.

Step 2: Confirm That the Website Received the Submission

Check the form platform, server logs, or browser developer tools, depending on how the form works. Look for the submission request and its response.

A successful response confirms only what that specific endpoint is designed to confirm. If the website sends data to an intermediate service, you still need to verify the next step.

Step 3: Check the Integration or API Response

Follow the request that transfers the form data to the CRM. Look for authentication failures, invalid field values, missing required data, rate limits, and server errors.

If the integration uses webhooks or an automation platform, review its execution history. Check whether the workflow ran, whether each action succeeded, and whether an error message explains the failure.

For custom integrations, make sure logs contain enough information to diagnose failures without exposing passwords, access tokens, or unnecessary personal data.

Step 4: Search the CRM for the Test Record

Search for the test email across the relevant contact and lead records. Check for existing records, duplicate handling, assignment rules, and automation that may have changed the record after submission.

If the CRM rejected the request, use the available error details to identify the field or rule that caused the problem. For example, Microsoft's documentation on troubleshooting failed marketing form submissions explains how submission logs can help identify failures when records cannot be created or updated.

Step 5: Repeat the Test After Fixing the Cause

Once you've corrected the issue, submit another test and follow the same path. Confirm that the CRM creates or updates the expected record, the relevant fields contain the right values, and the lead appears in the correct place.

Also verify that analytics records the intended conversion. If the fix involves resubmitting failed submissions, check for duplicates before replaying them, since some systems may create another record when a submission is processed again.

How to Prevent Missing Leads From Becoming a Recurring Problem

Finding one missing lead is useful. Making sure the same problem doesn't quietly affect the next campaign is even more important.

A reliable setup combines routine testing, clear ownership, useful error logs, and regular checks between form submissions and CRM records.

Test Forms After Important Website Changes to Verify Lead Tracking

A form can break after a website release, a CMS update, a CRM field change, or an integration adjustment. Add form testing to the release process whenever a change could affect submission behavior.

Test the full journey, including the confirmation message, CRM record creation, required fields, lead assignment, and conversion tracking. A form that looks correct on the page still needs to pass data through every connected system.

Monitor Lead Tracking Errors and Failed Submissions

Make sure someone can see when a form integration fails. Depending on the platform, this could involve error notifications, automation logs, API monitoring, or alerts for failed workflow runs.

Choose a process that fits the site's complexity. A small site may only need regular checks and clear error notifications, while a larger marketing operation may benefit from automated monitoring and alerts.

The important part is to make failures visible. If the team discovers missing leads only after sales reports a problem, the website may have been losing opportunities for days.

Compare Form Submissions With CRM Records to Verify Lead Tracking

Review form submissions and CRM records on a regular schedule. Look for unexpected gaps, sudden changes in conversion counts, and forms that generate submissions but few usable contacts.

Compare equivalent measures wherever possible. Account for repeat submissions, updates to existing contacts, spam filtering, and differences in how each platform counts conversions.

Give the process a clear owner. Marketing may own campaign reporting, while engineering or a WebOps lead monitors the integrations and investigates technical failures. Both teams should know who responds when the numbers stop matching.

Keep Changes to Forms and Integrations Documented

Record important changes to form fields, CRM mappings, API connections, validation rules, and automation. When a problem appears, the team can check what changed and narrow down the cause more quickly.

This is a practical part of website operations: the forms, analytics, and integrations that support marketing need ongoing care, just like the pages visitors see.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my website form say submitted, but the lead doesn't appear in my CRM?
A successful form message confirms that a specific step has completed, but it doesn't always mean the CRM saved the lead. The integration may have failed, the CRM may have rejected the data, or duplicate rules may have prevented a new record. Check the submission logs, integration response, and CRM records to identify where the process stopped.

How can I check whether my website form is connected to my CRM correctly?
Submit a test lead using a unique email address, then follow it through the form handler, integration, and CRM. Confirm that the request succeeds, the required fields map correctly, and the expected record appears in the CRM. Also check assignment rules and automation to make sure the record reaches the right place.

Can Google Analytics track a lead that never reaches the CRM?
Yes. Analytics can record a conversion when a visitor clicks a submit button or reaches a confirmation page, even if a later integration request fails. To improve lead tracking, define what counts as a successful conversion and compare analytics events with CRM records. Remember that repeat submissions and updates to existing contacts can also cause differences in the totals.

What are the most common causes of missing leads in a CRM?
Common causes include failed API requests, expired credentials, incorrect field mappings, missing required values, duplicate rules, and CRM automation that changes or redirects records. Reporting filters and permissions can also make a lead difficult to find. Checking each stage of the form-to-CRM process helps narrow down the cause.

How can B2B SaaS teams prevent leads from disappearing?
B2B SaaS teams can reduce missing leads by testing forms after relevant website changes, monitoring integration errors, checking CRM field mappings, and comparing form activity with CRM records. Clear ownership also matters: marketing, sales, and engineering should know who monitors the process and who investigates when submissions fail.

Final Thoughts

A form can look healthy on the website while the process behind it quietly loses leads. That's why reliable lead tracking needs more than a confirmation message or a conversion event. The full journey, from the visitor's submission to the CRM record, needs to work as expected.

When a lead goes missing, trace one test submission through each system, inspect the logs, and confirm what happened inside the CRM. Once you find the cause, add the right checks and monitoring so the same problem doesn't go unnoticed during the next campaign.

For B2B SaaS teams, this is an important part of WebOps. The website, forms, analytics, and CRM integrations all support the path from marketing activity to sales conversations. Keeping those connections healthy helps teams make better decisions and gives sales a more reliable stream of leads.

articles.body_html:
Slopsquatting: 1 in 5 AI Code Samples Recommends a Package That Doesn't Exist

Typosquatting needed you to make a mistake. Slopsquatting doesn't need you at all. The model makes the mistake, and the attacker just registers the result.

The name comes from Seth Larson at the Python Software Foundation: typosquatting, minus the typo, plus the slop.

If you use an AI coding assistant, you've seen this. It invents a package. Something plausible: strutils-pro, or a very official-sounding secure-random. The install fails, you shrug, you move on.

That failed install is the good outcome. The bad one installs cleanly, because someone else got to the name first.

One In Five, Measured

The largest measurement we have comes from researchers at UT San Antonio, the University of Oklahoma, and Virginia Tech, presented at USENIX Security 2025. They generated 2.23 million code samples with 16 code-generating models, Python and JavaScript, and checked every import against the real PyPI and npm registries.

19.7% of the samples contained at least one package that does not exist.

Not deprecated APIs. Not broken code. Fabricated import statements, delivered with full confidence.

That's 440,445 samples carrying 205,474 unique invented names. The spread matters as much as the total: open-weight models hallucinated packages at 21.7% on average, commercial models at 5.2%. CodeLlama-family models crossed 33% in some configurations. The best performer, GPT-4 Turbo, still sat at 3.59%.

Pick your favorite model. At the volume your team generates code, even the best rate is a weekly event.

The 2026 Check: Quieter, Not Fixed

In May 2026, an independent researcher re-ran the same methodology against five frontier models released between October 2025 and March 2026, across 199,845 prompts validated against the full PyPI and npm package lists.

Hallucination rates landed between 4.62% and 6.10%. The gap between best and worst collapsed from roughly tenfold to nearly nothing. On the surface, that reads as progress.

Then there's this: 127 package names that all five models invent identically.

Not similar names. The same names, from models built by different companies on different training runs. After coordinated disclosure to PyPI Security, 53 of them were still registrable by anyone with an account and a few minutes.

Five independent models agreeing on the same fiction means an attacker doesn't need to predict one model's quirks. Register the shared hallucination once, and every assistant in the ecosystem points its users at it.

Someone Ran the Attack for $496

In 2026, a research team did the thing everyone assumed someone would eventually do. They extracted 107 hallucinated package names from eight prominent LLMs, uploaded them to npm, and watched for six months.

The entire campaign cost an estimated $496.

35.2% of the installs came from real developers, with most first interactions landing within two weeks of registration. And 25.2% of the invented names sat within one character of a real package, close enough to survive a casual glance even when somebody checks.

One more finding worth sitting with: adding web search to the generator made it worse. Hallucination persistence rose from 11.2% to 17.3%, because the search results were themselves contaminated with AI-generated content. The tool we add to reduce hallucinations can quietly launder them.

Why Agents Move This From Nuisance to Attack Path

A human who types pip install usually glances at the name. Usually. An agent doesn't glance. It resolves dependencies as part of the task, installs them, and reports success.

The failure mode moves from "annoying error I noticed" to "dependency I never saw."

The Cloud Security Alliance stopped hedging in April 2026: treat every AI-recommended dependency as untrusted input. Not a suggestion. Not a shortcut. Input from a source that is confidently wrong several percent of the time, and real attackers have already started registering names to catch it.

Four Checks That Close the Door

None of the defenses are exotic. The CSA guidance collapses into four checks:

1. Verify before install. Does the package exist on the registry? Was it registered before your project started? Does the publisher have a history, or was the name claimed last month?

2. Treat lockfiles as load-bearing. Commit them, verify hashes on install, and build from the approved lockfile, not from the agent's enthusiasm.

3. Agents get an allowlist. If your coding agent can install packages, it installs from a list a human approved. Everything else escalates.

4. Generate an SBOM. If a large share of your code and dependencies arrived by generation, you need a manifest that says what's actually in the build.

The first check is small enough to run in CI:

# the model suggests; the registry decides
import sys
import requests

REGISTRY = "https://pypi.org/pypi"

def exists(name: str) -> bool:
    return requests.get(f"{REGISTRY}/{name}/json", timeout=10).status_code == 200

suggested = ["requests", "fastapi", "pydantic", "strutils-pro"]  # from the agent
for pkg in suggested:
    if not exists(pkg):
        sys.exit(f"blocked: '{pkg}' is not on PyPI, a human looks at this one")

💡 Pro-tip: a hallucinated package that fails to install is the system working. The dangerous one is the hallucination that succeeds, because it stopped being a hallucination the moment someone registered it.

The Part I Can't Shake

I keep coming back to the 127 shared names more than the 19.7%.

The rate tells you how often a model slips. The shared names tell you the slips aren't random. Different companies, different training data, converging on the same invented package. That is a property of the ecosystem, not of any one vendor. Switching models doesn't fix it. Blaming your vendor definitely doesn't.

For twenty years, supply-chain attacks needed a human to typo, click, or skip a check. Now the typo happens inside the model, at machine speed, several percent of the time, and the click is optional.

Have you caught your assistant suggesting a package that didn't exist? Did you verify it, or did the failed install do the verifying for you?

References

  1. Churilov, The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort (2026): arxiv.org/abs/2605.17062
  2. Huang et al., Package Hallucinations as Phantoms in Open-source Software Supply Chains, ACM TOSEM (2026): dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3830237
  3. Cloud Security Alliance, Slopsquatting: AI Code Hallucinations Fuel Supply Chain Attacks (April 2026): labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org. The CSA note documents the USENIX Security 2025 measurement used above, plus the full mitigation guidance.

articles.title: The CRDT That Throws Itself Away: Inside Eg-walker

articles.body_html:
Here's a number from a recent systems paper that stopped me cold.

Take the real editing history of Git's own Makefile, reconstructed from the Git repository, with its many authors and branches. Merge it with a classic Operational Transformation algorithm, and it takes one hour. Merge it with an algorithm called Eg-walker, and it takes 24 milliseconds.

Eg-walker comes from Joseph Gentle and Martin Kleppmann, in the paper Collaborative Text Editing with Eg-walker: Better, Faster, Smaller, presented at EuroSys 2025. What makes it interesting isn't just the speed. It's the trick behind it: a CRDT that only exists for the duration of a merge and is then thrown away.

If you've worked with collaborative editing, you know the trade-off this breaks. Let's look at how.

The trade-off everyone has lived with

There are two families of algorithms for collaborative text.

Operational Transformation (OT) stores the document as plain text and transforms concurrent operations against each other. It's memory-light and loads instantly, which is why Google Docs, Microsoft Office, and Overleaf use it. The problem is merging. If two users each made n edits while apart, every edit from one side has to be transformed against every edit from the other. That's at least O(n²), and some OT algorithms are cubic or worse. Fine for real-time typing with small n. Painful for offline work or long-running branches.

CRDTs give every character a unique ID and store positions relative to other IDs. Merging long branches is fine, and they work peer-to-peer. But that metadata has to be loaded from disk and held in memory the entire time a document is open, even when nobody else is editing. The paper measured that even the best CRDTs today use more than ten times the memory of OT just to view and edit a document.

So you pick: slow merges, or heavy documents.

Insight 1: store the history, not the state

Eg-walker starts by changing what gets stored and replicated.

Instead of CRDT metadata, every replica keeps an event graph: a DAG of every edit, where each event holds three things. An ID, the IDs of its parent events, and the operation exactly as the user performed it. That means plain index-based operations like Insert(3, "l") or Delete(1), never transformed, never rewritten.

If that sounds like Git, it should. The parents of an event record what its author had seen when they made it. Two events are concurrent if neither is an ancestor of the other, just like two commits on different branches.

This gives a clean definition of the problem. The document is simply:

document = replay(eventGraph)

where replay is a deterministic function. Any two replicas with the same set of events must produce the same document. Everything else is about making replay fast.

Insight 2: you only need a CRDT when there's concurrency

Here's the observation the whole algorithm rests on.

When you type locally, your edit's parent is the current state of the document. When a remote edit arrives that was made after everything you already have, its parent is also the current state. In both cases, there's nothing to transform. The edit's index is already correct, and you can apply it directly to a plain string.

Transformation is only needed when concurrent events meet. And in most real editing histories, concurrency is rare. Authors take turns, or there's only one author.

So Eg-walker keeps three things per replica:

  1. The event graph, on disk.
  2. The document, as plain text, in memory. No metadata at all.
  3. An internal CRDT state, which is temporary. It's built only to merge concurrent edits and then discarded. It's never saved to disk and never sent over the network.

Most of the time, the third item doesn't exist.

How replay works

When concurrent events do need merging, Eg-walker walks the event graph in topological order and builds its temporary CRDT as it goes. The clever part is that the CRDT tracks the document at two versions at once:

  • The effect version: the document with every event processed so far applied. This only moves forward.
  • The prepare version: the document exactly as the author of the current event saw it. This moves backward and forward.

Why two versions? Because an event like Delete(1) means "delete whatever was at index 1 in the author's view." To find the right character, you need the author's view (prepare). To know where that character sits in the real merged document, you need the full view (effect).

Each character gets one record in a list, including deleted ones. Each record holds two small states:

  • Prepare state: NotInsertedYet, Ins, or Del n (deleted by n concurrent deletions in the prepare view).
  • Effect state: Ins or Del.

And three operations move things around:

  • apply(e): interpret e in the prepare version, update both versions, and output the transformed operation for the real document.
  • retreat(e): make the prepare version behave as if e never happened.
  • advance(e): make e take effect in the prepare version again.

A walkthrough

Let's use the paper's own example. The document starts as hi. One user changes it to hey. At the same time, another user capitalizes it to Hi. After syncing, someone adds !.

Event Operation Branch
e1, e2 Insert h, Insert i shared start: hi
e3, e4 Insert(0, H), Delete(1) user B: Hi
e5, e6, e7 Delete(1), Insert(1, e), Insert(2, y) user A: hey
e8 Insert(3, !), parents: e4 and e7 after merging

Replaying in order:

  1. Apply e1 to e4. Each event's parent is the previous one, so nothing to adjust. The internal records are H, h (deleted), i, and the real document is Hi.
  2. Before e5, retreat e4 and e3. User A never saw B's edits, so the prepare version must forget them. H becomes NotInsertedYet, and h becomes Ins again. The effect state doesn't change: the real document is still Hi.
  3. Apply e5, e6, e7. A's Delete(1) is interpreted against A's view, hi, so it deletes i. A's inserts land after h in the record list. But when converted to the effect version, they're counted relative to the real document, which contains H. The real document becomes Hey.
  4. Before e8, advance e3 and e4. e8's author had seen both branches, so B's edits are brought back into the prepare view.
  5. Apply e8. Insert(3, "!") is interpreted against Hey, and the result is Hey!.

Notice what happened in step 3. A's Delete(1) was index-based, written against a document that never existed on B's machine. Retreating and advancing let the algorithm reconstruct exactly the view A had, at the cost of a few state flips.

A toy implementation

Here's a deliberately simple version in JavaScript, about 80 lines for the core. It skips all the performance work (more on that below), but it follows the algorithm's structure: topological sort, prepare/effect states, retreat/advance, and transformed output.

const NOT_INSERTED = -1, INS = 0; // sp: -1 not yet inserted, 0 inserted, n>0 deleted n times

export class EventGraph {
  constructor() { this.events = new Map(); }
  add(e) { this.events.set(e.id, e); return e; }

  // Lamport timestamp: one more than the max of the parents
  lamport(id) {
    const e = this.events.get(id);
    if (e._lt === undefined) e._lt = 1 + Math.max(0, ...e.parents.map(p => this.lamport(p)));
    return e._lt;
  }

  ancestors(ids) { // a version plus everything that happened before it
    const out = new Set(), stack = [...ids];
    while (stack.length) {
      const id = stack.pop();
      if (out.has(id)) continue;
      out.add(id);
      stack.push(...this.events.get(id).parents);
    }
    return out;
  }

  topoSort(shuffle = false) {
    const children = new Map(), order = [], seen = new Set();
    for (const e of this.events.values()) {
      for (const p of e.parents) {
        if (!children.has(p)) children.set(p, []);
        children.get(p).push(e.id);
      }
    }
    const visit = (id) => {
      if (seen.has(id)) return;
      if (!this.events.get(id).parents.every(p => seen.has(p))) return;
      seen.add(id); order.push(id);
      const kids = [...(children.get(id) || [])];
      if (shuffle) kids.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5);
      for (const k of kids) visit(k);
    };
    const roots = [...this.events.values()].filter(e => e.parents.length === 0).map(e => e.id);
    if (shuffle) roots.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5);
    for (const r of roots) visit(r);
    return order;
  }
}

export function replay(graph, { shuffle = false } = {}) {
  const order = graph.topoSort(shuffle);
  const pos = new Map(order.map((id, i) => [id, i]));
  const records = [];       // temporary CRDT: one record per character, incl. tombstones
  const target = new Map(); // event id -> record it touched
  let prepare = [];         // current prepare version
  let doc = '';             // the real document (effect version)

  const cmp = (a, b) =>     // total order on events: Lamport timestamp, then agent
    graph.lamport(a) - graph.lamport(b) ||
    (graph.events.get(a).agent < graph.events.get(b).agent ? -1 : 1);

  const nthVisibleInPrepare = (n) => {
    let seen = -1;
    for (let i = 0; i < records.length; i++)
      if (records[i].sp === INS && ++seen === n) return i;
    return -1;
  };
  const effectIndex = (recIdx) =>
    records.slice(0, recIdx).filter(r => r.se === INS).length;

  for (const id of order) {
    const e = graph.events.get(id);

    // 1. Move the prepare version to e.parents
    const oldSet = graph.ancestors(prepare), newSet = graph.ancestors(e.parents);
    const toRetreat = [...oldSet].filter(x => !newSet.has(x)).sort((a, b) => pos.get(b) - pos.get(a));
    const toAdvance = [...newSet].filter(x => !oldSet.has(x)).sort((a, b) => pos.get(a) - pos.get(b));
    for (const x of toRetreat) {
      const r = target.get(x);
      r.sp = graph.events.get(x).type === 'ins' ? NOT_INSERTED : r.sp - 1;
    }
    for (const x of toAdvance) {
      const r = target.get(x);
      r.sp = graph.events.get(x).type === 'ins' ? INS : r.sp + 1;
    }

    // 2. Apply e, interpreting its index in the prepare version
    if (e.type === 'ins') {
      let i = e.index === 0 ? 0 : nthVisibleInPrepare(e.index - 1) + 1;
      // Tie-break among concurrent inserts at the same spot (RGA-style rule)
      while (i < records.length && records[i].sp === NOT_INSERTED && cmp(records[i].id, id) > 0) i++;
      const rec = { id, ch: e.ch, sp: INS, se: INS };
      records.splice(i, 0, rec);
      target.set(id, rec);
      const at = effectIndex(i);
      doc = doc.slice(0, at) + e.ch + doc.slice(at);   // transformed op: insert at `at`
    } else {
      const i = nthVisibleInPrepare(e.index);
      const rec = records[i];
      target.set(id, rec);
      rec.sp += 1;
      if (rec.se === INS) {
        const at = effectIndex(i);
        rec.se = 'del';
        doc = doc.slice(0, at) + doc.slice(at + 1);    // transformed op: delete at `at`
      }                                                // already deleted elsewhere: no-op
    }
    prepare = [id];
  }
  return doc;
}

And a tiny helper to record edits the way a real editor would, with each event's parents set to whatever its author had seen:

export function makeAgent(graph, name) {
  let seq = 0, frontier = [];
  return {
    get frontier() { return frontier; },
    set frontier(f) { frontier = f; },
    ins(index, ch) {
      const e = graph.add({ id: `${name}${++seq}`, agent: name, type: 'ins', index, ch, parents: frontier });
      frontier = [e.id];
    },
    del(index) {
      const e = graph.add({ id: `${name}${++seq}`, agent: name, type: 'del', index, parents: frontier });
      frontier = [e.id];
    },
  };
}

Now replay the walkthrough:

const g = new EventGraph();
const a = makeAgent(g, 'a'), b = makeAgent(g, 'b');

a.ins(0, 'h'); a.ins(1, 'i');           // shared start: "hi"
b.frontier = a.frontier;

b.ins(0, 'H'); b.del(1);                // B: "Hi"
a.del(1); a.ins(1, 'e'); a.ins(2, 'y'); // A: "hey"

a.frontier = [...b.frontier, ...a.frontier]; // A syncs with B
a.ins(3, '!');

console.log(replay(g)); // "Hey!"

Every operation in the graph is stored exactly as typed. replay produces Hey!. Run it with { shuffle: true } and you get a different traversal order but the same result.

Two honest caveats about this toy. It uses a simple RGA-style rule to order concurrent insertions at the same position, while the authors use a variant of the Yjs algorithm designed to avoid interleaving concurrent runs of text. And it replays everything from scratch with linear scans, which brings us to the part that makes the real thing fast.

Insight 3: critical versions let you forget

A critical version is a point in the history where everything before it happened before everything after it. No branch crosses it. In a linear editing session, every single version is critical.

The paper's key observation is that critical versions split the history into independent sections. Events before one can't affect how events after it are transformed. That enables two optimizations:

  • Whenever replay reaches a critical version, the entire internal state can be thrown away. It's replaced with a single placeholder record meaning "some unknown text is here."
  • If an event and its parent are both critical, it's emitted unchanged. No CRDT work at all.

So when a concurrent edit arrives later, Eg-walker doesn't replay from the beginning of time. It finds the most recent critical version before the concurrency, starts from a placeholder, replays only the events since then, and applies the new ones.

For a document that's mostly edited by one person at a time, that means almost the entire history is skipped.

What the benchmarks show

The authors tested on real editing traces: sequential writing, real-time collaboration, and histories reconstructed from Git repositories. They compared their Rust implementation against Automerge, Yjs, their own optimized reference CRDT, and an OT implementation.

  • Merging long branches: On the Git Makefile trace, OT took an hour while Eg-walker took 24 ms, about 160,000 times faster.
  • Sequential editing: Eg-walker was 7 to 10 times faster than their reference CRDT, which itself outperformed both Yjs and Automerge.
  • Memory: In the steady state, while a document is open for editing, Eg-walker used 1 to 2 orders of magnitude less memory than the best CRDT.
  • Loading: Like OT, a document loads as plain text, orders of magnitude faster than the CRDTs tested.

The trade-offs

It isn't free, and the paper is upfront about where it costs.

Peak memory during a merge is CRDT-sized. While merging, Eg-walker's peak memory is roughly comparable to a CRDT's steady state. It's only cheap between merges.

Heavily concurrent histories gain little. On traces with constant concurrency, merge time was similar to their reference CRDT, because there are few critical versions to exploit. One trace had none at all.

Traversal order matters. On highly concurrent histories, a poorly chosen topological order made merging up to 8 times slower. The real implementation uses a heuristic to avoid that.

The worst case is O(n² log n). The authors note it's unlikely in real editing histories, but it exists.

You still store history. The event graph must be kept as long as concurrent edits might still arrive. It compresses well, but it's a cost.

It's plain text, for now. The paper covers plain text only, and the authors believe the approach can extend to rich text and other formats. That's not trivial: the team behind the Loro library, which draws on Eg-walker's ideas, has written that the original Peritext rich-text algorithm couldn't be used on top of it directly.

Why it matters

For years, the practical advice was: if you want lightweight, fast-loading documents, use OT and a central server. If you want offline editing and peer-to-peer sync, use a CRDT and pay for it in memory.

Eg-walker suggests that was a false choice. Keep the immutable history, keep the document as plain text, and build the CRDT only for the moment you actually need it.

If you want to dig deeper, the authors' production Rust implementation lives in Diamond Types, and there's a TypeScript reference implementation written for readability. The paper itself is very readable too.

I'm curious whether anyone here has run into the OT vs. CRDT trade-off in production. Which side did you pick, and would something like this have changed your decision?

articles.body_html:
Most of us have the "don't commit secrets" reflex drilled in. Pre-commit hooks, secret scanners in CI, .env in .gitignore. Good. That covers the repo.

It doesn't cover the context window.

The gap: the repo is not the boundary anymore

When you work with an AI coding assistant, what leaves your machine isn't just the file you're editing. It's whatever you paste, whatever the extension decides is relevant, and whatever the agent reads while it's "helping." The security boundary now includes the editor extension, the chat history, any telemetry, and every service that processes that context on the way to the model and back.

Secret scanners watch commits. Nothing in a typical setup watches what you paste into a chat panel at 6pm while a deploy is failing.

Here are the usual ways a secret ends up in context without ever touching git.

1. The failing test that prints its config

An integration test fails. The assertion message helpfully dumps the client object, which includes the connection string with the password inline. You copy the whole test output into the assistant and ask "why is this failing?"

The question was about the assertion. The payload included the credential.

2. The environment dump 

$ env | sort
...
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:...@db.internal:5432/prod
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_...

"Here's my environment, why can't the app find the config?" is a completely normal debugging move. It's also the fastest way to hand over every key on the box in one paste. Agents that can run shell commands can do this on their own if you let them.

3. Logs that log too much

A verbose HTTP client logs request headers. One of them is Authorization: Bearer .... You paste 200 lines of log to get help with a timeout, and line 143 is a live token.

4. The copied snippet

Someone shares a "working example" in Slack with the key still in it. You paste it into the assistant to adapt it. Now it's in two systems you don't control instead of one.

(These are illustrative scenarios, not specific incidents, but if you've debugged anything under pressure you've probably seen at least one.)

What actually helps

  • Minimize what you send. Paste the relevant ten lines, not the whole log. Ask about the error, not the environment.
  • Redact before pasting. Mask tokens, connection strings and headers. A small shell function or editor snippet that scrubs obvious patterns is worth having.
  • Scope your credentials. If a dev key does leak, it should only be able to touch dev. Short-lived, least-privilege keys shrink the blast radius.
  • Check how your tool handles data. What's retained, for how long, whether it's used for training, what the extension sends automatically, where telemetry goes. These are often separate settings and separate policies. One "privacy" toggle rarely answers all of them.
  • Restrict what agents can read. If your assistant can open files and run commands, keep .env, credential files and secret stores out of its reach.

If it already happened

Deleting the chat message is not remediation. You don't know what was logged, cached or forwarded before you hit delete. Treat it like any other exposure: rotate the credential, revoke the old one, check access logs for use.

The reframe

Secret management used to be a version control problem. With AI tools in the loop, it's a data-flow problem: anything that reaches the model's context has, to some degree, left your control.

The safest secret is the one that never enters the context in the first place.

How does your team handle this today? Do you have any tooling that checks what goes into an AI assistant, or is it all down to developer habit?

articles.title: 92 Green Field Tests Meant Nothing Until I Counted Which Could Lie
articles.description: The v0.2.0 field test for agentwatch ran 94 cases across 15 suites. 92 passed. 0 failed.  It was the...
articles.body_html:
The v0.2.0 field test for agentwatch ran 94 cases across 15 suites. 92 passed. 0 failed.

It was the least trustworthy green I'd ever shipped. Not because anything was failing — because I couldn't say why it was passing.

So I did a census. Of the 94 case assertions, how many could fail if the claim they were checking turned out to be false?

The answer was about 8.

The census

Every case had a step script. I read all 94 and sorted them into shapes:

Shape Count What it proves
Driver runs, prints ok: ..., exits 0 52 The commands executed
